en: *Collected Works of Xianjin*, Scroll One, composed by the Śramaṇa Qisong of Mount Dongshan in Xianjin, Tengzhou. Part One:
*Supplement to the Teachings* (1–3). Upper Section: *Supplement to the Teachings*, Part One.
Fundamentally, all things possess nature and emotion;
throughout antiquity and the present, there is birth and death.
Yet, regarding this birth, death, nature, and emotion—
There has never been a case where things exist without being mutually dependent.
Death is certainly dependent on life;
life is certainly dependent on emotion.
Sentiment is fundamentally rooted in nature.
That which causes the myriad things to drift and sink within birth and death is the burden of sentiment.
The Sage possesses a grand vision;
he traces its cause back to before birth,
thereby demonstrating the reason for its coming.
It points to that which is accomplished after death and teaches the means by which to cultivate it;
thus, it guides the world with this Way.
To cast aside emotions and falsehoods in the present is to provide the necessary foundation for certain success in the future.
Such is the nature of life.
Since there are already the past and the future, and they interact with the present, do these not constitute the three periods of time?
One brings about the goodness of the future by means of what is cultivated in the present.
Thus, it can be clearly seen from what has transpired that one’s current state of adversity or success is determined by what one has previously practiced.
Emotion is that which issues forth from nature;
all such [issues] are emotion.
If emotions and habits possess goodness or evil, [then so do the results].
When it undergoes transformation, it is obscure and dark;
it forms through mutual resonance with its own kind.
That which is thus formed may have emotions and habits that are thin.
There are those who are sincere;
among these, there are those whose capacities are great and those whose capacities are small.
The Sage approved of this;
therefore, he set forth its methods as the Five Vehicles and the Three Piṭakas.
Branching out further from the five vehicles,
its proliferation is nearly beyond counting;
at its highest level, it perfects the holy path.
Down to the most mundane among secular activities— those who are farmers, merchants, artisans, physicians, and those engaged in the humble labors of the hundred crafts—
he demonstrated the underlying principles of each.
Furthermore, these, together with the five vehicles, are all subsumed within the Three Baskets (Tripitaka).
To cite its most prominent aspects, it is headed by the five vehicles.
The first is called the vehicle of humans;
the next two are the vehicle of devas.
The next three are called the Śrāvaka-yāna;
the next four are called the Pratyekabuddha-yāna;
and the next five are called the Bodhisattva-yāna.
As for what are called the "three vehicles" mentioned later,
they were intended to lead their followers to transcend the mundane world.
They enabled them to thoroughly cleanse themselves of defilement and proceed directly toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The spirits communicate with it;
the world cannot fathom it.
As for what is called the two vehicles mentioned previously:
Because worldly sentiments are deeply ingrained and their desires cannot be abruptly removed,
one must regulate them by working with those very sentiments.
This is what is called the "Human Vehicle," which refers to the Five Precepts.
The first is non-killing.
This means one should love living beings and must not recklessly harm a single creature;
it does not merely mean abstaining from eating their flesh.
The second is non-stealing.
This means not taking what is not rightfully one's own,
nor seizing or pilfering the property of others.
The third is to refrain from sexual misconduct,
which means not to engage in illicit relations with those who are not one's spouse.
The fourth is to refrain from false speech.
That is to say, not to deceive others with one's words.
Fifth is not drinking alcohol;
that is to say, not to allow intoxication to disturb one’s cultivation of the mind.
It is said that the Celestial Vehicle consists of the expansion of the five precepts, which are called the ten wholesome actions.
The first is: not killing.
The second is not to steal.
The third is not to engage in sexual misconduct.
The fourth is not to speak falsely.
The meaning of these four is the same as that of the five precepts.
The fifth is called "avoiding frivolous speech," which means not engaging in talk that glosses over one's faults.
The sixth is refraining from double-tongued speech;
that is, speaking to people in their presence rather than behind their backs.
The seventh is refraining from harsh speech.
This means not reviling others, nor speaking what is unrighteous.
The eighth is non-envy,
which means being free from jealousy and resentment.
The ninth is non-anger,
which means not harboring resentment or malice in one's heart.
The tenth is non-delusion.
This means not being ignorant of good and evil;
yet, it is said that by practicing these ten together,
one is thereby reborn in heaven.
The cultivation of the first five [perfections] is that by which one becomes a true human being.
If all under heaven were to cultivate each of these accordingly, [the world would be transformed].
Even assuming that one is not born in heaven, if every person were to fully accomplish goodness,
and if every person were good, it has never happened that the world would not be well-governed.
Formerly, Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty said to his minister He Shangzhi:
I recently saw the treatises composed by Yan Yanzhi and Zong Bing,
which elucidate the Buddha-dharma with great clarity and reason;
both serve to inspire and encourage the human spirit.
If those along the shores of the entire realm were all to be moved by this transformation,
I would then sit with hands folded and achieve Great Peace;
what further affairs would there be?
Shangzhi then continued, saying:
"In a village of a hundred households,
if ten people observe the five precepts, those ten will become pure and conscientious."
In a village of a thousand households,
if a hundred people practice the ten wholesome deeds, those hundred will live in harmony;
by extending this moral instruction throughout the entire world, peace shall prevail everywhere.
If there are a billion households, there will be a million benevolent men.
Now, if one can practice a single good deed, one eliminates a single evil;
if one eliminates a single evil, one brings rest to a single punishment.
When punishments cease within the family, they cease throughout the state.
Thus, Your Majesty’s statement that "peaceful prosperity can be achieved simply by sitting still" is precisely correct;
these words have captured the truth.
If one examines this by comparing it with Confucianism,
then what they call the "Five Constants" (wuchang) of benevolence and righteousness are merely different names for the same essence.
Now, benevolence and righteousness are the records of the governance of the former kings for a single generation.
If one judges them by these traces,
they have never failed to differ.
Inferring by means of principle,
they have never failed to be identical;
the traces emerge from the principle.
Yet principle is the ancestor of its traces;
traces are the branches while principle is the root.
It is appropriate for the gentleman to seek the root and set aside the branches.
The saying goes:
"Examine what they do;
observe the way they proceed."
Examine what they find comfortable.
How can a person hide anything?
How can a person hide anything?
Mencius said:
"If one does not examine its base and level its top,
even a piece of wood a foot square can be made higher than a lofty tower."
This means that one must first evaluate the root of a matter and align its branches before speaking of it.
To judge the principles of the three periods of existence based solely on the traces of a single lifetime is improper.

How is this different from taking a shoe that has traveled ten paces and questioning one that has traveled a hundred paces, saying: "Why are your tracks so numerous? Why do you not make them as sparse as mine?"
How could one know the distance of their destination or the extent of their steps?
Nevertheless, when sages establish teachings, they expand upon them according to differing circumstances;
these words pertain to a single age.
Thus, one should accord with human sentiments to govern the interval between the physical form and life.
To speak of the three periods [of past, present, and future],
one should rectify the relationship between the human spirit and its objects, pointing toward the conditions of karma beyond birth and death.
Shennong recorded the hundred medicines; though they differ, they are the same in their healing of disease.
Houji identified the hundred grains;
though they are distinct, [they are the same in nourishing life].
Yet they are the same as those who serve at meals.
The sages differ in their methods of instruction,
yet they are the same in their aim for goodness.
It is said that the Way of the Buddha governs the three periods of time;
it is not something that can be grasped by the ears or eyes.
By what means, then, do you clarify it?
I say: when a person dies, their spirit does not die.
This is the proof.
The spirit's presence in a person is like fire in wood.
Although the preceding fuel was consumed by the fire, how could that which is now called "fire" ever have been consumed?
It is said: the divine principle is profound and subtle.
Once its form has perished,
who can restrain where it goes?
Is it truly a human being?
Are they not, then, of different categories—those that fly and those that hide?
It may be said that this can be reconciled;
for if one infers by means of their emotional dispositions and the karma of their habitual tendencies, [the distinction becomes clear].
Thus, their retribution is unfailing.
Have you not heard of what is called the "Five Blessings and Six Extremes" in the *Hongfan*?
As for the Five Blessings:
This means that when a person brings their mind into accord with the August Ultimate,
Heaven responds by using these five [virtues] to encourage them toward it.
As for the six extremes:
This means that when people do not align their hearts with the August Ultimate,
Heaven employs these six [calamities] to respond by restraining them with awe. Thus,
while their physical forms remain, the retribution for their good and evil deeds has already been realized.
If that spirit departs, how could it not be the case that there is retribution for good and evil?
A Buddhist sutra says:
"All phenomena arise in form through the mind."
This is what is meant by that.
It is said that the Buddha-way consists in severing emotions, yet its practice is such as this—
is it not, then, emotional?
Does the Buddha also possess sentience?
[The interlocutor] replies: "By 'sentient beings,' one refers to those who possess form and appearance.
Is the Buddha alone devoid of sentience?"
The Buddha’s conduct is devoid of *qing* (sentimental attachment);

it is merely that he acts without such attachment. It is asked: since the Buddha’s actions resemble those of benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*), how can benevolence and righteousness not be called *qing*?
It is asked in reply: What is benevolence?
This is what is meant by "kindness and love.
What is meant by "righteousness" (yi)?
It is what is meant by "appropriateness to the occasion."
It is appropriate that both love and its opposite arise from one's nature and manifest in their function;
how could they not be rooted in emotion?
Speaking of them in terms of their emotional nature:
Thus, benevolence and righteousness are the goodness of human emotion.
When one acts out of emotion, its tendency approximates expediency;
when one acts without emotion, its tendency approximates principle.
Natures are identical, while dispositions differ.
When they differ, few in the world do not compete;
when they are identical, few in the world do not find peace.
The Sage desires to lead them toward that which they find peace in,
thereby extending their innate nature to harmonize with all living beings;
the Sage desires to bring rest to that which they strive for.
Therefore, that which is extended through its embrace throughout the myriad things is called "things" (wu).
There are no insects, nor anything moving or stationary.
The Buddha bestows it upon all equally and without partiality or diminution;
this is called "birth."
Without distinction between noble and base, or wise and vulgar,
the Buddha treats all as one and guides them,
causing each to seek [enlightenment] for themselves; by extending their own nature, they become identical with all living beings.
Can this not be called Great Sincerity?
To extend one's inner being so that it fully encompasses all things—
can this not be called Great Compassion?
Because of great compassion, its influence upon people is profound;
because of great sincerity, its transformation of beings is easy.
Thus, from within the Middle Kingdom to beyond the four barbarians and the eight tribes of the south, [the Way prevails].
When those people heard the Buddha’s words—
that doing good brings merit and doing evil incurs guilt—
few failed to comprehend them; they restrained their evil intentions and joyfully cultivated their wholesome thoughts.
I have guarded his teachings with such earnestness that I dare not lose them.
As for what were previously called the five precepts and ten wholesome acts,
how is it that they are not already being transformed into practice throughout the villages and lanes?
From the village to the town;
from the town to the district;
from the district to the state.
Among the scholars of the court and within the inner palace of the Son of Heaven,
their cultivation reaches its ultimate point:
they do not kill and are necessarily benevolent.
If one does not steal, they will surely be upright.
If one does not commit lewdness, they will surely be correct.
If one does not speak falsely, they will surely be trustworthy.
One does not become intoxicated or disordered.
One avoids frivolous speech and remains sincere;
one refrains from double-tongued talk, slander, and harsh words, and does not bring humiliation upon others.
Without anger or resentment;
without envy or contention;
without delusion or ignorance.
If possessing even one of these is sufficient to cultivate sincerity within oneself and extend it to others,
how much more so when the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds are complete?
How could there be one who is a younger brother yet fails to be filial toward his elder brother?
To be a son and yet not be filial toward one's parents;
to be a wife and yet not be respectful toward her husband;
to be a friend and yet not promote goodness toward one another.
For there to be a minister who is not loyal to his sovereign,
or a sovereign who is not benevolent toward his people—
such a thing does not exist in the world.
Those who practice it only fear falling into the extremes of excess or deficiency as a personal eccentricity.
How could the Buddha have indulged in such a mere eccentricity toward others?
If this were so, how could the Way of the Buddha be the private concern of a single individual?
Moreover, they surely have their intentions regarding the world, the state, and the family.
How could they ever fail to maintain the bonds between ruler and subject, or father and son?
How could this hinder the way by which people are nurtured and sustained?
However, that which issues forth does not originate from the officials who propagate it;
rather, the principle of its transformation is subtle and difficult to perceive.
Therefore, the world cannot place full confidence in it.
The *I Ching* says:
"To accomplish it through silence and to command belief without speaking depends upon one's virtuous conduct.
Mencius said:
"The people daily migrate toward goodness without knowing who causes it to be so—
is this not indeed the case?
Humanity has long been deluded by its emotions."
When human feelings reached such an extreme that they were nearly ruined and impoverished,
the ancient sages were concerned about this;
they established laws so that people would govern one another.
They call him the Emperor;
they call him the King.
Although his Way has many aspects, [it remains one].
Yet they still do not have the leisure to rescue them,
to treat them with benevolent kindness,
or to instruct them with righteousness.
Rewards are intended to encourage the good;
punishments are intended to deter the evil.
Although punishments cause increasing toil and rewards cause increasing expenditure, [they must still be applied].
Yet, as worldly customs grow increasingly thin,
if one hears of someone who wins over the people and leads them toward goodness and away from evil without relying on rewards and punishments—
even one as sagely as Yao or Shun would surely rejoice and strive to achieve such a thing.
How could one say that if this person does not perform good deeds because of my Way, I shall not accept their goodness?
One must wait until they perform good deeds through my Way before their goodness can be accepted.
If this were so, it would mean that the sage is being partial toward his own Way.
How could there be anything private about the Way of the Sage?
When a dragon glides through the rivers and seas, vapors rise up in profusion from all sides;
when a tiger roars in the mountains and forests, whistling winds come sweeping in.
For it is their own kind that naturally corresponds with one another.
Thus, a good person is welcomed by other good people even if they are not kin;
and a wicked person is tolerated by other wicked people even if they owe him no favor.
Shun delighted in inquiry and examined even the words of those nearby;
he concealed their faults while proclaiming their virtues.
Upon hearing a single virtuous word or seeing a single virtuous deed, he would act accordingly.
"If one dikes the Yangtze and the Yellow River, their surging waters cannot be resisted.
When Yu heard virtuous words, he would bow in reverence.
Confucius once said:
"I cannot find a truly good man to see.
It would be enough for me to find one who possesses constancy.
He further said:
When three people walk together, there is bound to be someone from whom I can learn.
I shall choose what is good in them and follow it;
as for what is not good, I shall reform myself accordingly.
When Yanzi obtained even one instance of goodness,
he would earnestly take it to heart and never dare to lose it.
Mencius said:
To love what is good excels throughout the world.
It is further said:
"There is a way to cultivate sincerity within oneself."
Those who do not understand what is good have failed to be sincere in their persons.
These five gentlemen—
The great music of antiquity was virtuous;
because its virtue accorded with that of the Buddha, it would surely be categorized as such.
If it does not perish, it shall be seen as a transmission of our Way.
This must surely lead to a state of total oblivion as one follows along by mere inference.
Alas! This is the misfortune of later generations:
they are unable to encounter one another and provide mutual verification.
Yet this causes the followers of both schools to remain hesitant and fail to trust one another.
Alas! Among human beings, there is none who does not cherish their own views while neglecting those of others, esteeming this while disparaging that;
unless they find fault, they do not engage in debate.
To be exclusively devoted leads to confinement;
the gentleman seeks only to be comprehensive.
Why must he be dogmatically exclusive?
The gentleman should simply act with propriety;
why must he insist on what is not right?
As for food, drink, and the affairs of men and women, everyone is capable of knowing their value.
Yet the gentleman does not prize this.
That which the gentleman prizes is that one is able to know the Dao and recognize the underlying principle.
Now there is this Great Way and its profound principles;
yet I have failed to recognize them.
I am deeply ashamed before others for this.
An attempt at discourse:
Now, if one wishes for people’s hearts to be won over so that they cultivate themselves spontaneously, nothing is better than moving their inner selves;
if one wishes for people’s words to be compliant and their outward conduct to follow, nothing is better than regulating their external selves.
To regulate the external,
if one does not establish teachings through the Way of humanity, one cannot achieve the desired result.
To move the internal...
If one does not establish instruction through the Way of the Divine, transformation cannot be guaranteed.
Therefore, as for the Way of the Buddha,
it begins with the divine and subsequently proceeds to the human.
This is what is meant by "moving the internal and thereby regulating the external.
As for "spirit" (shen),
it refers to the spirit and consciousness of a person.
This does not refer to matters of ghosts, spirits, lust, or delusion;
rather, it means that when a person cultivates their spirit and refines their conduct,
blessings will respond during their lifetime.
If one dies with such a state, the spirit ascends in purity;
yet if one does not cultivate the spirit and practices what is perverse and deluded,
then even if one lives, it is no cause for celebration.
When they die, their spirits shall suffer punishment;
thus, when the world hears of this, their hearts will be moved:
the wicked will be deterred, and the virtuous will follow suit.
In this way, through silent transformation, there has been no era in which such a thing did not exist.
Nevertheless, when its teaching was established within the Middle Kingdom,
it must have been because it accorded with the suitability of the times and arrived in response to the resonance of the human heart.
Otherwise, how could it be that when people cultivate according to this method,
Heaven and Earth respond to them and the ghosts and spirits manifest their efficacy?
If it were indeed appropriate, yet the full extent of its numerical principles had not been exhausted, [how could such results have occurred]?
Since the principle of mutual resonance has not yet been fully exhausted,
how can one merely preserve what is liked or discard what is disliked as a matter of convenience?
If we compare this to human affairs, it is like a sovereign who governs:
he acts in accordance with the seasons and responds to the needs of the people; how could this not be so?
How much more so when it comes to the wondrous Way and its hidden skillful means, as well as human affairs?
As for what is called the "wondrous Way":
This refers to what is called pure quiescence.
It means that one has extinguished all burdens and returned to the state of original purity.
It does not mean the death of life or the pursuit of a void, desolate, and absolute extinction.
By reaching this state, one becomes a sage and spirit who transcends their world;
this is what is called "dark power" (mingquan),
which refers to arising through the Way from the function of non-function.
This refers to those who rescue and uplift all sentient beings, leading them out of their immersion in emotional attachments.
Examining how they transform others through self-transformation, one finds that the Imperial Way (Huangdao) is nearly realized therein.
Examining the application of their skillful means in responding to the world, there is nothing they cannot reach.
As for its transformation,
later generations will certainly be unable to reach it;
as for its power, if one silently embodies it, there is no age in which it cannot be attained.
In ancient times, when the sages were about to pass away,
they entrusted their methods to kings, ministers, elders, and those who possessed strength.
This was not out of self-interest, nor merely to show honor to others.
This is because one wishes to take their Way as one's own Way and their goodness as one's own goodness;
for the scriptures of the Buddha are indeed manifold.
The followers of later generations were unable to bestow teachings upon others with propriety.
Those who sought to inspire faith overtrusted them,
causing Your Majesty to desire to abandon the kingdom and become a slave to those who were merely flatterers and sycophants.
In common worldly practice, there are those of shallow understanding who hastily wish to abandon their vocations to specialize solely in the excellence of the monastic life;
this is not what is meant by employing the Buddha-mind to cultivate the Way.
Does the Sūtra not say:
The Buddhas teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each, and their underlying intentions are difficult to comprehend;
therefore, to be a Buddha does not consist merely in blackening one's robes and shaving one's hair.
Yet, such is the mind of a Buddha.
How could such a thing be considered a minor attainment?
There are those who wish to criticize this by comparing it to the doctrines of Yang Zhu and Mo Di.
Now, as for Yang Zhu and Mo Di:
To remain stagnant in a single doctrine and be constrained by worldly customs—
to compare such a state with that of the Buddha—
is it not an extreme disparity?
The world does not investigate the Buddha’s principles to examine them in detail;
instead, it merely clamors in confusion, slandering the Buddha and claiming his teachings are unorthodox.
Yet the Buddha’s insight transcends that of ordinary men by far.
How can one, because they have not seen it themselves, disparage what others have seen?

To claim that the Buddha’s words regarding *kalpas* are extravagant is to ignore that in this world there are indeed accumulations of months that form years, and accumulations of years that form ages.
Furthermore, how can one know that the accumulation of ages does not constitute a kalpa?
If, simply because a matter is remote and beyond the reach of one's ears and eyes,
one were to claim it is not so, [one would be mistaken].
Thus, regarding the matters of antiquity set forth in the Six Arts,
if one does not receive their transmission now,
who else could have personally witnessed them?
Can this be called extravagant?
Is it extravagant to say that the Buddha’s words are great?
Indeed, there have always been those in the world whose minds wander through the void and travel therein.
Although the four corners, the zenith, and the nadir appear profound and remote, how could they ever have a limit? The Buddha called his world "infinite"; why should this not be so?
To say that the Buddha’s words are mere transformations and thus false is absurd.
In this world, there are indeed those who dream within a dream; at the very moment they are dreaming, [they perceive it as real].
The events encountered, the body and life, and the circumstances—
whether they are identical or different— are all analogous to dreams.
Once one is within a dream, it is already a dream.
Furthermore, how can one know that within death there is not transformation?
Since the Buddha’s vision is far-reaching and his knowledge of things is manifold,
the Sage broadened his teachings to instruct many different classes of beings.
I desire that there be nothing to which one is attached, so as not to be transformed by it.
Now you say that the Buddha was a sage of the West and that his teachings are suited for the barbarians but not for China.
This is something that the former scholars had not yet considered.
A "sage" (shengren) is essentially a designation for one who possesses the Great Way.
How could there be one who possesses the Great Way yet cannot be called a sage?
And how could there be the Way of a sage that cannot be put into practice wherever it reaches?
If it is argued that this is because the person originated from a foreign land, [then the answer follows].
If Shun was a man from the eastern barbarians and King Wen was a man from the western barbarians,
yet their Way met and succeeded one another, being practiced throughout the Middle Kingdom.
Can one therefore exterminate its people and reject its Way?
Moreover, the origin of Buddhism is not among the "barbarians" (Yi).
Someone said:
The Buddha merely speaks of "nature" (*xing*).
Since nature is easily [attained], it is as described in the Doctrine of the Mean;
there would be no need for the Buddha to exist.
This, too, is not so.
As for the nature of our Buddha’s words,
they are identical to those of worldly books.
This is because the sages share the same nature.
When they share the same [nature], they set aside differences; but how do they deal with those who are different?
When water finds its commonality in abundance, it becomes deep as rivers and seas.
When soil finds much that is like it, it accumulates to form mountains and peaks;
when great men find much that is like them, they expand to embody the Way and its Virtue.
Alas! How can I find many others who are like me?

They unify their hearts in sincerity, unify their bodies in fasting and purification, and unify their efforts in promoting virtue to others, so as to bring blessings to their parents and provide for the health of their ruler’s governance of the world. One might ask: "Why do you not grow weary of this? [The answer is: It is because it is the way of Heaven. Thus, one who practices this is called a sage. This is what is meant by "the Way of Heaven. Therefore, the sage does not consider his own body as his own; he considers the people as his own body, and he considers all things as his own body. He does not consider his own life as his own; he considers the lives of others as his own life, and he considers all things as his own life. Consequently, he does not rejoice in his own life nor feel resentment toward death. He does not value gain nor loathe loss. He does not delight in long life nor fear early death. He does not welcome fortune nor shrink from calamity. He does not exult in success nor despair in failure. He does not rejoice in being praised nor resent being slandered. He does not take pride in being honored nor feel dejected when disgraced. He does not feel joy when he has something, nor sorrow when he lacks it. He does not feel elation when he is wealthy, nor distress when he is poor. He does not feel glad when he is noble, nor sad when he is lowly. He does not feel happy when he is praised, nor unhappy when he is criticized. He does not feel joyful when he is loved, nor sorrowful when he is hated. He does not feel glad when he is trusted, nor distressed when he is distrusted. He does not feel happy when he is strong, nor sad when he is weak. He does not feel glad when he is right, nor sad when he is wrong. He does not feel glad when he is wise, nor sad when he is foolish. Thus, it encompasses all existence and animates all movement.
Therefore, if one embodies and preserves it,
it is as if one has returned to its very source.
To illuminate and employ it—
does this not resemble its outward manifestation?
Yet when the mind is merged with the ultimate source, it is truly within that state.
To remain silent, pure, and to transcend the sage while discarding wisdom—this too is appropriate.
It is what is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya): vast, empty, and quiescent.
If there were no sages, who would know what is erroneous?
Yet the people of Qin consider [the doctrine of non-being] to be excessive and far-fetched, not conforming to human nature.
If there were no sages, who would know that which is non-existent?
This, too, does not yet clarify its subtle purport.
As for the cognitive awareness of ordinary beings and sages,
it is merely the shadow of the ultimate truth and the clinging of the deluded mind.
To abide in shadows and echoes is to become stagnant within names and numbers;
to rely on攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective conditions) is to be dazzled by discrimination.
Thus, it is not being a sage that makes one a sage, but rather [transcending these states].
Therefore, the Great Sage knows through non-knowing; this is his true knowing.
This is why he possesses universal knowledge.
Long ago, someone asked another person:
"What is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)?
The latter should have replied:
Vast and open, there is no sage.
A questioner asked:
"Who is it that stands facing me?"
He replied,
"I do not know him.
However, this man does not fail to recognize the Sage out of ignorance or obstinacy."
It is because I do not wish for people to seek the ultimate truth through forms and words; yet,
when my interlocutors fail to awaken to this,
they continue to speak at length.
"To mark the boat while seeking the sword":
this is indeed far-fetched.
Using a finger to point at the moon—the finger exists for the sake of the moon.
One uses words to elucidate the Way;
thus, the words exist for the sake of the Way.
Yet, people look to the words while neglecting the Way itself.
This is not knowing the Way.
It is like looking at the finger and not looking at the moon;
it is not recognizing the moon.
Therefore, the Perfected Person constantly attains wondrous enlightenment beyond words and images,
and uniquely realizes the truth outside of the physical form.
When Vimalakīrti remained silent, Mañjuśrī praised it as excellent.
Śāriputra speaks by means of non-speaking;
Śakra hears by means of non-hearing— is this not so?

2. Discourse on the August Ultimate (4):
That which is shared equally by all under heaven is called the Great Publicity.
That which is the central and correct standard for all under heaven is called the August Ultimate.
Centrality and Rectitude are what unify the hearts of all things;
it is not Centrality and Rectitude that cause the hearts of all things to become alienated.
If they were alienated, the world would fall into chaos.
To unify them in this way, the world will be well-governed.
One who excels at governing the world must first uphold the Great Ultimate (Huangji) and realize the Great Public Good (Dagong).
Those who govern the world unskillfully must first abandon the Imperial Ultimate and discard the Great Public Spirit. Therefore,
the sages of antiquity promoted the Imperial Ultimate to the sovereign.
It was none other than his desire to govern the world.
This is what he taught as the ultimate principle for the people.
It was none other than his desire for the world to be well-governed.
As for the court, the state, and the nation—
This is the great principle of the world.
Wealth, honor, and high status are the great trends of the world.
If one maintains it by attaining its Way, then its physical form and momentum will be strong;
if one maintains it by losing its Way, then its physical form and momentum will be weak.
This Way is none other than the Way itself.
This is the Way of the Imperial Ultimate (Huangji).
The Wen and Wu kings of Zhou quelled and eradicated calamities and chaos, restoring the great royal enterprise.
Possessing wealth, honor, and loftiness, they were succeeded from father to son.
It was divined that the dynastic line would endure for many generations and that its years would be long; indeed,
from antiquity to the present, none has ever surpassed it.
The fame of his meritorious virtues was brilliant and resplendent,
its radiance spreading throughout the infinite.
This is what is meant by "upholding [the Dharma] and attaining its Way."
When the realm was pacified and order restored,
he descended from the hall to personally pay court to the feudal lords;
yet when the capital was moved eastward, he merely sought to evade the Rong and Di tribes.
The feudal states are arrogant and defiant, yet he cannot restrain them;
wealth, honor, and high status abound, yet he cannot command respect.
Alas! His great legacy from the former kings stands precariously on the verge of collapse.
This refers to those who uphold [the Way] yet lose its true course.
Alas! A family of but a few members possesses five mu of land, yet each man and woman presides over it as their own.
He was extremely simple in his personal conduct and extremely meticulous in his governance; yet,
when he presided over them with impartiality and integrity, [all were transformed].
Therefore, their family members were drawn to them,
and their neighbors admired them.
The prosperity of such a household could even be passed down through successive generations to their descendants.
How much more so when one possesses the great framework of the world,
rides upon the great momentum of the world,
and has the resources necessary to achieve success.
There is a momentum that makes it easy to achieve;
if one employs the Imperial Mean (Huangji) to promote it, who would not follow and submit?
"Is it not the case that they return with shoulders brushing and feet treading upon one another?
As the poem says:
'The virtuous person, the noble gentleman.'"
They are indeed the people of the state;
they are indeed the people of the state.
Why should they not live for ten thousand years?
This is what is meant by that.
Someone asked:
"What is the Way of the Imperial Ultimate?"
It is said: "The Way of Heaven,
the Way of Earth,
and the Way of Humanity— these three powers are permeated and unified as one."
He asked, "What does this mean?
He replied, "If the Way of Heaven is not upright and central,
then the sun, moon, and stars will not be bright."
Wind, rain, frost, and snow do not arrive at their proper times;
the five elements are disordered, and the myriad things fail to flourish.
The Way of Earth is neither central nor correct.
Then the mountains, peaks, and hills will collapse;
the Yangtze, Yellow, Huai, and Ji Rivers will freeze over;
and the grasses, trees, and hundredfold fruits will fail to ripen.
The city walls and dwellings all collapsed.
People said that because the Way was not centered,
their natures and emotions fell into chaos.
Within, they act with delusional arrogance; without, they inflict calamity and harm.
Thus, they injure their own lives and injure others as well.
Therefore, although Heaven is lofty, brilliant, and vast,
were it not for the subtle Imperial Ultimate (huangji),
what would Heaven be? Although the Earth is broad, thick, and boundless, [what would it be without the Imperial Ultimate?]
Without the Imperial Ultimate (Huangji), what would constitute the ground?
Although humans receive the refined essence and are more spiritual than the myriad things,
without the Imperial Ultimate, what would constitute humanity?
Therefore, the Imperial Ultimate (Huangji) was not created by the sages;
it is rather the principle that Heaven and Earth have always possessed.
Thus, when humans lose the Imperial Ultimate, the transformations of Heaven and Earth follow suit.
The sage is one who attains the Imperial Ultimate before others;
therefore, he infers from it to instruct his people.
Yi Yin said:
I am one who has awakened first among the people of Heaven.
I shall use this Way to awaken these people.
A sage is precisely what is meant by one who has awakened first.
Therefore, as for why the sages were so cautious regarding the Imperial Pivot (huangji),
it was because of their earnest dedication to the welfare of humanity and the profound depth of their concern for the world. Why is this so?
Since the time of Shun and Yu, successive generations have grown increasingly degenerate.
Among the clamorous and garrulous, who is without fault?
At the very least, they err within their own households.
When the great exceeds its proper bounds within a state,
and when the even greater exceeds its bounds throughout all under heaven,
the Imperial Axis (Huangji) is thereby used to rectify them.
It was only then that [the system] began to be implemented across the Nine Categories (jiǔchóu).
King Wu obtained it and thereby established the realm of Zhou.
Thus, the empire became both vast and enduring.
Thus, the five blessings and six calamities are tied to the Supreme Ultimate (Huangji) of the individual person;
the auspicious omens and baleful omens are tied to the Supreme Ultimate of the state and the whole world.
How could the Imperial Ultimate be abandoned?
Alas! There is no one who does not use a balance and scale to rectify the lightness or heaviness of gold, nor draw a plumb line to rectify the crookedness or straightness of wood.
Regarding the means by which one governs oneself, as well as the state and the realm,
if one does not know to uphold the August Standard (Huangji) to rectify them,
this is the wisdom of sages, worthies, and heroes.
Consequently, he ends up below the master craftsman and all other artisans.
Mencius said:
"This is a matter of not doing it."
It is not that they were incapable;
for when the ancient rulers— indeed, the "junzi"— undertook any action,
they took up the Imperial Ultimate (huangji) and put it into practice.
Therefore, he is neither hesitant nor indecisive;
he does not rely on spirits for deliberation nor consult others for judgment.
Even if Yao were to hand over the empire to such a person, [he would do so without hesitation].
Yet the people of the world did not resent Yao for not treating his own kin as he did others;
nor did they resent Yu for bestowing the empire upon his son, even though he thereby showed partiality toward his own kin.
Tang’s first campaign began with Ge,
yet the whole world placed its trust in him;
when he campaigned facing east, the western barbarians grumbled in envy.
When he marched southward, the northern Di tribes felt resentment,
saying, "Why does he leave us behind?
The people gazed upon him as those suffering from a great drought long for clouds and rainbows.
Yet the world did not resent Tang for the hardships of his military campaigns,
because he shared [the benefits] with the world.
Shun, though a common man, received the mandate over the world.
The Duke of Zhou enfeoffed more than fifty states for his kinsmen throughout the empire;
yet neither Shun nor the Duke of Zhou ever allowed their private interests to cast doubt upon the world.
Furthermore, the world considers both Shun and Duke Zhou to have been impartial toward all under heaven. Under the Zhou,
there were ten ministers who brought disorder,
yet their state was well-governed.
Zhou had billions of common people, yet why did his state perish?
It was because he employed the Mean and the Right; thus, it is not necessary to have many.
If one acts without rectitude and impartiality, what benefit is there even if one does much?
He asked, "What is meant by acting with rectitude and impartiality?
He replied, "Entrusting great talents with great affairs."
Those of minor talent should be entrusted with minor affairs.
Those capable of great tasks must not be discarded because of a minor failure;
those suited for minor matters must not be burdened with great responsibilities.
The poem says:
"On the mountain there are hazel trees; in the marsh there is the wild asparagus. Of whom do I think?"
The beauty of the West.
O, that beauty! She is a person of the West.
This is because Zhou’s employment of men was comprehensive, ensuring that both great and small found their proper place.
Rewards, punishments, dismissals, and promotions are the sovereign's great powers;
proclamations, edicts, penal codes, and laws are the sovereign's great teachings.
If the teachings are not centered and upright, the people will be suspicious;
if the means of governance are not centered and upright, the prevailing power will be deceptive.
One asks: what is meant by the centrality and uprightness of both the means and the teachings?
It is said: Rewards are the means by which public interest is advanced;
they are not bestowed with excessive favor based on partial affection.
Punishments are the means by which private interest is suppressed.
One does not increase the gravity of a penalty on account of someone's base or wicked character;
those who are dismissed are so punished for the sake of correcting their transgressions.
One does not apply two different standards to the law based on whether a person is noble or humble.
Ascending is for the purpose of ascending one's path;
one does not examine a person by means of slander or praise.
Issuing commands is for the purpose of stabilizing the people.
One must not issue laws lightly and then repeatedly alter them.
Penal law is meant to restrain the people;
it should not be promulgated in excess nor applied with excessive severity.
If one is overly cautious and solemn, others will become weary and feel no sense of gratitude;
if one acts lightly and changes frequently, others will be confused and find no standard to follow.
If one examines a person based on their detractors and eulogizers, those driven by love or hatred will be able to indulge their words unchecked.
If one differentiates the rites based on the distinction between noble and base, those of high station will come to rely upon their power.
If one increases the weight of the rites out of mere expediency or ill-will, the failure lies in a lack of benevolence (*ren*).
If one adds greater thickness to the rites out of mere expediency or affection, the failure lies in a lack of ritual propriety (*li*).
Ritual is the outward manifestation of the Imperial Ultimate;
music is the sound of the Imperial Ultimate;
and institutions and regulations are the instruments of the Imperial Ultimate.

If one does not rectify their vessels, then the well-field system will falter, taxes will become disordered, and the upper classes will overstep their bounds while the lower classes will encroach upon them.
If one does not sustain their sounds, then humans and spirits will be in disharmony and social customs will drift into decadence.
If one does not manifest their proper demeanor, then there will be no distinction between the honorable and the humble, and superiors and subordinates will become entangled with one another.
Now, the Imperial Standard (Huangji) does not exist because of antiquity, nor is it absent because of the present;
it does not endure merely because of the era of Yao, Shun, Yu, or Tang.
It does not vanish because of [the reigns of] Chuan, Zhou, You, or Li;
it depends solely on the one who practices it.
When the practice reaches its ultimate, [it endures].
It is by this that one becomes an Emperor or a King;
yet if the practice has not reached its ultimate fulfillment,
one becomes one of the Five Chiefs or a feudal Lord.
To sever [the passions] and not act upon them is what leads to the ruin of a state;
to attain [this cessation] is to be a sage.
One who practices these is a worthy person.
To discard them and fail to learn is to be a petty man.
Someone said:
Did the Qin and Han reach the ultimate realization of the Imperial Ultimate (Huangji)?
One might say that although the fall of the Qin state need not be discussed further, the failure of its grasp on the Imperial Ultimate is clearly discernible.
As for the Han dynasty’s relation to the Imperial Ultimate:
If one examines his calligraphy, each stroke can be clearly distinguished;
yet, speaking of it in general terms, it does not reach the ultimate perfection found in the works of Wang Xizhi.
It lies somewhere between the two.
Or perhaps one might think this is so.
3. Commentary on the Zhongyong (4). 1. First, Commentary on the Zhongyong. Part One. Someone may say:
"The Zhongyong and the Liji appear to be different works."
Now, ritual (*li*) is that by which distinctions of rank are ordered and systems of regulation are recorded.
As for the Doctrine of the Mean (*zhongyong*):
"This is merely a matter of rectifying the discourse on nature and destiny (*xing-ming*).
Does this not differ from the various ritual classics?
The old man followed by explaining it, saying:
Do you not know of the Doctrine of the Mean?
This Doctrine of the Mean is indeed the ultimate point of ritual propriety and the source of benevolence and righteousness.
Ritual, music, penal law, government, benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, and trustworthiness—
these eight are unified in the Mean.
When humans lose their innate nature and come into contact with external objects, [they fall away from it].
Thus, joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, and hate arise;
cravings and desires are unleashed.
Then there was a sage.
Fearing that the principles of Heaven would perish and human relations would fall into disorder,
he established ritual, music, penal law,
and government to regulate joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate, and desire.
He establishes benevolence, righteousness, wisdom,
and faithfulness to broaden his teachings and Way;
he establishes ritual propriety.
There are superiors and inferiors, insiders and outsiders;
thus, those who bring joy may not be treated with undue intimacy,
and those who provoke anger may not be treated with undue distance.
To provide music for them,
there are refined, upright, and harmonious sounds to harmonize with their vital breath,
ensuring that those who seek pleasure and indulge in desires do not fall into excess; this serves as a means of moral restraint.
There are executions, punishments, demotions,
and reprimands; these are established as governance so that those who become angry and give vent to evil shall not be able to oppress one another.
There are rewards and punishments,
so that those who grieve may have their grievances heard and those who fear may be encouraged;
this is what it means to practice benevolence.
To teach them to be broad-minded and generous so as to tolerate all things is righteousness;
to teach them that in undertaking affairs they must always act with appropriateness is propriety.
To provide for them is wisdom;
to teach them to be open and flexible while knowing how to adapt is faithfulness;
to teach them to speak so as not to deceive is trustworthiness.
Therefore, ritual, music, criminal law,
and government are the great regulations of the world;
benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, and trustworthiness are the great teachings of the world.
If the manifestation of emotions does not exceed their proper measure,
and the cultivation of conduct does not deviate from its instruction,
then the Way of the Mean may be approximated.
Now, the Mean is the Way by which humanity is established. Therefore,
when a gentleman is about to take action, he acts with this in mind.
When one is about to undertake an action,
one must first cultivate the Mean and the Righteousness before proceeding.
Even the consumption of food and drink may be discontinued for this purpose.
The power of wealth, nobility, and high status may be relinquished,
but the Mean (zhongyong) must not be abandoned.
This is because one who perfects their heart through sincerity [must maintain it].
Those who cultivate themselves;
those who rectify their households;
and those who govern their states.
As for those who manifest brilliant virtue throughout the world,
if they did not rely on the Middle Way, what else could they have relied upon?
As for those who cause their states to perish and themselves to be destroyed, it is because they failed to follow this path.
This is surely because they have forgotten the Middle Way (*zhōngyōng*).
As the Book of Documents says:
"The Way (*dào*)..."
"One must not be separated from it for even a moment;
that which can be separated is not the Way. Is this not what is being referred to?"
2. The Second Explanation of the Doctrine of the Mean. A second questioner asks:
"What are called ritual, music, penal law, and government are the great regulations of the world.
Benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, and trustworthiness are the great teachings of the world."
If the expression of emotions does not exceed their proper measure,
and the cultivation of conduct does not deviate from its teachings,
then the Way of the Mean may be approximated.
"I am utterly bewildered and have not yet grasped its meaning.
Pray, sir, explain it to me once more.
The old man said:
"This youth has ambition;
he is capable of hearing the Way.
Now, as for instruction—"
Thus, in applying this to human beings:
the "measure" (jie) is that which regulates the emotions.
When benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, and trustworthiness are fully realized,
the fundamental order of human relations is established; when ritual, music, law,
and governance are cultivated, [society is brought to harmony].
Thus, human sentiments find their proper place;
people do not bring violence upon their lives,
and the natural order of human existence is preserved.
When the emotions do not disturb one's nature,
and the principles of human nature are rectified,
then the Way of the Mean (Zhongyong) is preserved therein.
Therefore, joy, anger, sorrow, pleasure, love, hate,
and desire are those things that lead people away from the Mean. Benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, faithfulness,
ritual, music, punishment, and government— [these are the means by which one returns to it].
It is that which guides people toward returning to the Mean.
Therefore it is said: benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, faithfulness, ritual, music, punishment, and government—these eight are unified within the Mean.
Now, that which is called the "Middle Way" (Zhongyong) is not something that can be contrived;
it is not something that can be confined to a single vessel.
It is luminous as the sun and moon, yet cannot be seen;
it is profound as ghosts and spirits, yet cannot be fathomed (some versions read "it is unfathomable").
Only the junzi can thereby preserve the Way through the Mean.
Only the petty person fails to do so.
Therefore, one who can transform through the Middle Way achieves perfection; such a person is virtuous.
Thus, there is nothing it cannot reach.
When transformation becomes non-virtuous,
likewise, there is nothing it cannot reach.
The Book says:
"Everyone says,
'I know how to choose the Middle Way,' yet they are unable to maintain it for even a single month."
How could these sages not desire that people begin and end their lives in the Middle Way, and be cautious regarding changes?
Shun employed this as a ruler,
and subsequent generations praised him as a sage.
Yan Hui employed this principle to serve as a minister,
and thus later generations praised him for his virtue;
King Wu and the Duke of Zhou employed it to serve as sons.
Subsequently, later generations praised him for his filial piety.
How could the *Zhongyong* be a mere fabrication?
Alas! As for those who become rulers of men in later ages...
For those who serve as ministers,
and for those who act as sons and grandsons,
that their descendants are not praised in later generations is due to nothing other than this.
This is because the Mean has not been cultivated.
Third, the third "Explanation of the Mean. Question Three:
The *Hongfan* says:
"The Sovereign establishes its ultimate mean.
Commentators say this means "he greatly establishes that which possesses the mean."
Is this then the same as or different from what you call the Way of the Mean?
I reply: It is largely identical with the Imperial Ultimate (Huangji), yet differs slightly.
They are the same because they both tend toward the substance of governance;
they are different because their methods of instruction differ.
The Imperial Ultimate is the teaching;
the Doctrine of the Mean is the Way.
As for this Way:
"It issues forth all things and enters back into all things;
therefore, the Dao is taken as the Mean.
Its "Doctrine of the Mean" says:
When joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness have not yet been manifested, it is called the Central (zhōng).
When they are manifested and all accord with the proper measure, it is called Harmony (hé).
This Centrality—
It is the great root of all under heaven.
Harmony is the universal path of all under heaven.
"When one attains the state of ultimate harmony and centrality, heaven and earth find their proper places;
does this not mean that one has entered into all things?"
Instruction is that which rectifies all things and straightens all things; therefore,
instruction is taken as the "Centrality."
The *Hongfan* says:
"Be without partiality, be without bias; follow the righteousness of the King.
Be without favoritism; follow the Way of the King."
There shall be no doing of evil, for one follows the path of the King.
Without partiality and without factionalism, the Way of the King is vast and wide.
Without factionalism and without partiality, the Way of the King is level and even.
Without reversal and without deviation, the Way of the King is upright and straight.
It meets with the ultimate and returns to the ultimate.
Is this not also the way to make all things upright?
Now, the Zhongyong and the Hongfan stand to each other as the exterior and the interior,
just as a person possesses a heart within.
If a person were without a mind, how could they give form to life?
If the mind were without a person, how could it exercise its functions of thought and deliberation?
He asked:
Zhengzi, in his commentary on the passage "That which Heaven mandates is called nature," states:
"Heaven's mandate refers to that which Heaven mandates for the production of human beings;
this is what is meant by 'nature and destiny' (xing-ming)."
The deity of wood is benevolence;
the deity of metal is righteousness;
the deity of fire is ritual propriety.
The spirit of water is wisdom;
the spirit of earth is faith.
Examining the meaning of Master Zheng, there remains some doubt.
If Heaven’s mandate brings forth human beings,
their nature arises from what they are moved by.
If they are moved by the spirit of wood, then their nature is benevolence (*ren*).
To be moved by the spirits of metal, water, fire, and earth is the nature of righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness;
it seems not something acquired through practice.
Is this not different from what you say—that benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness must necessarily be cultivated and perfected within their nature?
"I am fortunate to hear the reason for this.
The old man said,
"How delightful is your question!"
I have long been of the opinion that Zhengshi’s explanation is not thorough,
yet I have lacked the leisure to discuss it.
However, as for Zhengshi:
How could one possibly exhaust the discourse on nature and destiny?
Now, as for what is called "that which Heaven mandates is termed nature":
the mandate of Heaven is the numerical order of Heaven and Earth.
"Nature" (*xing*) refers to the spiritual intelligence (*xingling*).
This means that humans are born from the numerical patterns of Heaven and Earth and thereby unite with this spiritual intelligence.
Nature is the principle that has always been inherent.
It is because they possess emotions.

The Sage recognizes that human nature inherently includes affection and love, feelings of gratitude and resentment, the capacity for discernment and reflection, and the inclination toward compliance and pursuit.
Therefore, one may take their teachings and expand upon them:
through affection and love, one can fulfill the human bond;
through inspiration and emotion, one can fulfill righteousness.
Discernment can bring about ritual propriety;
reflection can bring about wisdom;
and following others can bring about trustworthiness.
Who is it that, through stimulus and response, attains its nature?
Now, before things have taken form,
neither nature nor life exists at all.
What is it that is capable of being moved?
Once a person has been born,
why must they wait for a spiritual entity to move them in order to possess their nature?
Those elements— gold, wood, water, fire,
and earth— are insentient things;
who could have repeatedly commanded them to be so?
How strange are the words of Zhengzi!
He has failed to reflect most profoundly. If his explanation were correct, [it would lead to such absurdities].
If this were so, what need would there be for the Sage to provide instruction?
Yet some remain silent and acquiesce to this.
Fourth, the Explanation of the "Doctrine of the Mean," Part Four. Someone says:
I have heard that human nature has its superior and inferior aspects,
just like the hands and feet.
It cannot be changed.
Thus Confucius said:
"Only the highest wisdom and the lowest folly are unchangeable."
The Master Han said:
"Those at the higher level do only good;
those at the lower level do only evil."
Mencius said: "In that case,
the nature of a dog is like the nature of an ox,
and the nature of an ox is like the nature of a human."
Yet, that which you call "nature" seems to imply there is no distinction between the worthy and the unworthy,
nor any difference between humans and beasts.
They are blended into one, such that their upper and lower parts cannot be distinguished;
thus the feet may be placed upon the head,
and the head may be set upon the feet.
To overturn it and turn it upside down—
how could one see anything therein that does not shift?
How do you differ from the teachings of the sages and worthies?
The old man said,
"Although I have discoursed with you all day long,
you remain obstinate and do not understand."
Is there nothing that can be done?
You have received my words but have not understood them with your heart;
do you still seek to hold me accountable for the matter?
"Though I am skillful at speaking,
how can I escape the condemnation of excessive talk?
Zhongni said:
"Only those of superior intelligence and the lowest of fools are unchangeable.
This means that among people, whether they possess talent or lack it is a fixed distinction.
Those who possess talent and clarity are superior;
those who lack talent and are obscured are not.
That they are "lower" does not mean that their nature is inherently superior or inferior. Therefore,
it was said previously:
"Nature is similar;
practice makes it different.
Yet, the superior intelligence and the inferior stupidity do not change."
Furthermore, if one were to claim that because human nature has superior and inferior grades that cannot be altered,
then the natures of food, drink, and sexual desire would exist only in the wise.
Yet the ignorant do not possess it.
If all were to possess it, one could not say that their natures are fixed as superior or inferior.
These are the words of Master Han.
To take the case of Zhongni (Confucius),
he is what is called "unchangeable.
It is because one cannot examine his significance in detail from afar that people hastily determine his rank based on good and evil.
Is this truly so?
Good and evil are matters of emotion;
they are not inherent nature.
Sentient emotions possess good and evil,
yet why is it that the nature is neither good nor evil?
It is because the nature is quiescent.
The emotions are what stir.
It is through this stirring that the forms of good and evil become manifest.
This is as Mencius said: "The nature of a dog is like the nature of an ox."
As for the claim that "the nature of oxen is like the nature of humans," Master Meng was likely referring to what the nature desires;
it is therefore appropriate that they differ.
What I speak of is nature;
