for this, I feel truly regretful.
For the time being, while we have not yet had the opportunity to meet in person,
may you have a million blessings and cherish yourself.
A letter from [Name] to Chan Master Yuantong regarding his resignation from the monastery.

Yesterday, a messenger arrived with your formal letter, which I have already received. I am deeply moved by your profound path here; for while your virtue is still in its prime and your years are young, why did you suddenly cause such a stir among the ears and eyes of the multitude?
Furthermore, having heard the opinions of both sides, I again request that you remain here for ten million kalpas and follow the public consensus.
I am but an old man of worn-out body and meager virtue;
I cannot serve as their leader or organizer.
The world knows well that Qian Dao was mistaken;
why did he take this man as his successor?
Regarding the sentiments of yielding and deference found in the *Qian* hexagram,
even one who is naturally eminent— how could a base and inferior person ever hope to master them?
I earnestly request that you set aside your noble intentions and remain for a short while for the sake of the assembly.
I am but an old and worn-out man from the east, west, south, or north;
I truly have no fixed abode.
I have no expectation of seeing you again for a long time to come; please take great care of yourself.
With profound respect, I, [Name], address this letter to the Elder Wanshou.

I am deeply honored that you have sent a messenger with your letter of consolation; this sufficiently demonstrates that you have not forgotten our long-standing bond. I am moved beyond measure, beyond measure.
It is regrettable that the Dharma Seal Abbot cannot be cured.
It eventually came to this;
moved by inconsolable grief,
he sought out a text to inscribe upon his stupa.
Although I am unworthy to be considered a close friend of yours, given our profound mutual affection, how could I possibly resort to formal refusals at such a time?
Moreover, with this pen of my own clumsy and straightforward nature, I shall briefly comply with your noble command,
thereby expressing the sincerity of our lifelong friendship.
Whether to adopt or abandon [these matters] further depends on your own discretion. May you increase your efforts tenfold as a guiding principle for others;
please take care of yourself.
This is sent in response with the utmost respect. Sincerely yours, [Name], respectfully addressing Elder Wanshou.

Although we have not been able to communicate through letters, my sincere admiration for the Way has only grown more earnest and diligent. Some say that my lack of virtue has become even more pronounced in old age;
during the spring season, I retired from public life, and as the Buddha-sun deeply set, I hid myself on Longshan.
In this desolate state, others cannot endure such sorrow, yet I have never grown weary of it myself.
I recently intended to send inquiries and listen to your teachings,
but Huainan has not yet returned.
Therefore, my purpose was not fulfilled.
However, having recently met with Lord Cao,
I learned that his daily life is pure and excellent.
I am comforted by your kind words regarding my solitary situation.
Having been advised by the unworthy [self], I intend to travel to Mount Lu to prepare for my journey;
I shall be the first to pay homage at the monastic center.
As the winter cold has not yet ceased, I pray that you will cherish yourself well.
I respectfully submit these humble sentiments and do not further elaborate.
A Memorial from [Name] to the Venerable Abbot Bao Yue of Hangzhou. I, [Name], respectfully address this memorial to the Venerable Abbot Bao Yue of Hangzhou.
Recently, as I grew old and was afflicted by illness, I requested leave from my duties as abbot.
I am deeply honored that you have deigned to visit me,
showing such extraordinary compassion and concern for my well-being.
I am deeply indebted to the members of the monastic community;
how can I sufficiently express my gratitude and shame?
Yet, as the summer retreat has not yet concluded, I have been unable to attend to the preliminary rites.
I respectfully submit this letter of thanks.
This is my reply to the letter received from the Abbot of Jinshan regarding the tea ceremony.
This morning, the Prior arrived and honored me with his written invitation.
He prepared exquisite delicacies at his own residence;
such diligent devotion born of affection is beyond words to describe, for he exhausted every sincerity of his heart.

Although I am not skilled in socializing with others, how could I dare to compromise my integrity and righteousness for the sake of today’s matter? I need not trouble you to assemble outside; as it is currently the height of the great heat, I inform you that we shall suspend this gathering. Written on the [day].
I respectfully send this person back with my letter.
I humbly hope for your compassionate regard.
To the Administrative Officer of Donglin, [Name] of Donglin.

I now humbly receive the report that you have dispatched a messenger from afar specifically to present this letter and inquiry. Since the time of the assembly of former sages and worthies, it has been my misfortune to remain in self-concealment; yet, that your gracious command should reach me from so far away is a singular and abundant honor.
A certain person has perversely gathered hollow reputations and further extolled your lofty integrity.
Reflecting upon my own folly, how could I possibly match such virtue? I am ashamed of my own decrepitude and exhaustion;
furthermore, being constrained by current affairs, I have been unable to attend promptly.
I am deeply ashamed and distressed that I have detained the messenger for so long;
my feelings of resentment and trepidation only increase.
As you return, I respectfully submit this letter to express my thanks; I pray that you will hold me in your compassionate thoughts.
On the sixteenth day of this month, the venerable Master Chu arrived and presented me with a gift of his calligraphic inscriptions.
I am delighted by the purity of his spiritual intent, which is free from all external entanglements.
In this world, leisure is the foremost thing;
do not allow the eyes of the vulgar to see it.
For the past year or two, I have found it most unpleasant even to hear of such matters.
When thought and deliberation are exhausted, there is nothing left to be endured.
As the ancients said, "A thousand miles share the same wind"—this is precisely what is meant. What you have asked, worthy brother, is not only foolish and deluded, but is also fundamentally inverted.
I have spoken at length on this matter;
your reply is like the wind passing through trees—
it does nothing but increase the din.
The illness is within the membranes and there is no way to remove it.
Although you, sir, possess the affection of a brother, what can be done? What can be done?
The Host of Offerings and the Donor [Name] address this to the Donor [Name]:
We have gathered these eminent companions, truly relying upon your noble generosity.
Although we have long admired your exemplary conduct, we now seek your support.
I have not yet had the opportunity to present this to your refined person;
my longing is but keen, yet the prospect of meeting you remains uncertain.
As the autumn air grows slightly clear, I pray for your continued well-being and care.
Respectfully submitted by Huaxingren, whose efforts are dedicated solely to this.
Not further expressed. *Tanjin Wencji*, Volume Ten.
Collected Works of Xianjin, Volume Eleven, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Qisong of Mount Dongshan in Xianjin, Tengzhou.
8. Prefaces (11). Preface.
Preface to the Chart of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma and the Fixed Ancestors:
It is said that Bodhidharma was indeed the twenty-eighth patriarch of the Buddha’s teaching,
following Mahākāśyapa.
This is the direct lineage transmitted from Śākyamuni Tathāgata himself.
As it was transmitted to China over many generations, the records have become confused and erroneous;
yet scholars, possessing little insight, have been unable to investigate and clarify its true origin.
Conflicting and divergent theories have prevailed throughout both ancient and modern times;
I have long regarded this as my greatest affliction.
I have now examined their right and wrong and rectified their fundamental principles.
Just as this book was about to be issued,
it coincided with the distribution of the "Diagram of the Patriarchs Transmitting the Dharma and Bestowing the Robe" throughout the world.
Although those who study Buddhism all honor this,
they remain bewildered and have not yet understood the Emperor’s intent. I,
[Name], am fortunate enough to venture to say this in private to those who are discerning:
Our Buddha takes the essential core of the True Dharma as the source of this Great Teaching;
he takes the secret transmission and reception [of the Dharma] as the progenitor of this Great Teaching.
This source is the fundamental origin of the Way of the sages and worthies.
It is the wondrous foundation of all living beings.
Its progenitor is the great paradigm for learning and cultivating wisdom throughout ten thousand ages;
it is the true verification of the teachings of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Since the confusion caused by the transmission of handwritten copies has rendered the texts obscure and blurred,
the world has harbored doubts for nearly a thousand years. Now, Your Majesty,
the Great Sage, has specially issued this diagram to rectify the lineage of its ancestral source.
However, as for the teachings of the Sage, only a Sage can rectify them.
Is this not not only the great good fortune of the followers of the Buddha for ten thousand generations,
but also the great good fortune of all living beings born within Heaven and Earth?
I, so-and-so, certainly do not avoid the punishment for my audacity and foolish presumption;
yet, daring to risk death, I venture to cite ancient accounts from this scripture to elaborate upon the intent of the Supreme Sage.

I have respectfully annotated the "Chart of the Patriarchs," which refers to what was previously distributed concerning the transmission of the Dharma and the conferral of the robe by the ancestral masters. However,
from its inception, it has confused our ancestral school and deluded the scholars of the world.
Nothing is more suitable than the *Dharmatrāta-dharmapada-śāstra* (Fu fazang zhuan) for rectifying the ancestral lineage;
nothing is more suitable than the *Dhyāna-sūtra* for severing the disputes of ten thousand generations.
The emergence of the *Dhyāna Sūtra* preceded the *Dharma-Transmission Chronicle* by sixty-two years;
it records the beginning and end [of the lineage] in full detail.
The twenty-eight patriarchs were already known during the Jin dynasty;
however, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fufa zang zhuan) is missing from the period following Emperor Zhu Shixing’s suppression of the Dharma.
It merely states that the twenty-fourth generation appeared during the Wei period.
It is precisely because of this that the *Chanding jing* (Sutra on the Experience of Dhyāna) and the *Fofazang zhuan* (Tradition of the Dharma-treasury) must be considered erroneous.
For if it were the case that the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma exclusively to Mahākāśyapa, [the aforementioned texts would be contradicted].
One may then perceive it in the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, the various dhyāna sūtras, and their prefaces.
By seeking it through the power of intention,
the subtle purport of the Buddha remains therein.
His supreme sagacity was lofty and sublime, uniquely attaining that which lies beyond words and concepts;
this was indeed his innate disposition as well as the Buddha’s prediction.
Therefore, when he expounded the patriarchs of Chan, it naturally accorded with the sutras.
It is fitting that this be handed down for ten thousand generations as a permanent and definitive judgment.
Let the disciples of the Three Studies follow it and look up to it;
then the world will no longer harbor doubts.
The figures listed therein extend from Śākyamuni Buddha and Mahākāśyapa down to the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi, Chan Master Dajian.
There are thirty-four individuals in total.
Furthermore, there are the worthies of both Confucianism and Buddhism who have spoken concerning the patriarchs of our school.
Those who have long possessed documented evidence—
these ten figures are placed to the left and right of the various patriarchs,
following closely the *Zhengfajingzongji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma).
I have come to the palace gate to present this;
having troubled Your Majesty’s august favor,
I cannot bear the extreme of my trepidation and fear.

A Humble Preface to the Record of the Dharma-Treasure of the Sixth Patriarch. This preface to the *Record of the Dharma-Treasure of the Sixth Patriarch* was composed by Lang Shilang. Attached herein is a note from the *Book of Tang*, which states:
"At the end of the Later Wei dynasty, there was a monk named Bodhidharma."
Originally the son of the King of India,
he left the household life to protect his country and entered the Southern Sea,
where he attained the wondrous Dharma of the Chan school.
From the time of Śākyamuni Buddha, there has been a succession of transmission,
using the robe and alms bowl as the seal of verification,
handed down from one generation to the next.
Bodhidharma brought his robe and alms bowl across the sea and arrived at the Liang court to visit Emperor Wu.
The Emperor questioned him regarding matters of conditioned existence.
Bodhidharma did not speak [of his destination];
he instead went to Wei and remained hidden at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song.
He transmitted his Dharma to Huike.
Sengcan may transmit it; Sengcan transmits it to Daoxin;
Daoxin transmits it to Hongren;
and Hongren transmits it to Huineng.
Furthermore, Shenxiu emerged from him;
he was able to serve as the sixth patriarch of Bodhidharma’s lineage in China,
and thus the world calls him the Sixth Patriarch.
The *Fǎbǎojì* records the Dharma taught by the Sixth Patriarch.
This Dharma is the fundamental basis of all living beings—
whether humans, spirits, or the myriad things.
Consequently, this [view] is in great and chaotic contrast with that which is pure,
clear, vast, and great. Out of compassion for this,
the Sixth Patriarch instructed people as follows.
If one wishes for others to seek it themselves,
one must turn back toward the Way from within their own minds. Yet,
those who speak of human nature and destiny (*xing-ming*) throughout the world are many.
If one’s words are most detailed,
one’s reasoning most correct,
and one’s inferences most exhaustive.
Yet the Śākyas have attained it;
for their demonstration of it is the ultimate in directness,
and their approach to it is the ultimate in directness.
The Sixth Patriarch was as closely related to the Śākya clan as one could be to a kinsman;
furthermore, regarding his attainment within the teachings and path of the Śākya tradition, the Sixth Patriarch [excelled].
This may be called essential and ultimate.
Now, the Record of the Kai-shan Pavilion by His Majesty the Emperor states that one realizes the definitive meaning through one's original nature.
There has never been anyone who, having abandoned the Way of the Sixth Patriarch, was able to reach this state.
Thus, the Sixth Patriarch is truly the compassionate father of the three realms and the virtuous heir of all Buddhas.
How magnificent!
Only the Most Holy One is able to know the Ultimate Way.
Nevertheless, I have long held the teachings of the Sixth Patriarch in the highest esteem.
He lamented that the text had been altered by popular custom,
its characters being so vulgar, coarse, and redundant as to be nearly impossible to verify.
It was during this time that the śramaṇa Qisong composed the *Zantan jing zan* (Eulogy on the Platform Sūtra).
He said to Master Song,
"If you can rectify this,
I shall provide the funds."
He commissioned woodblock printing to broaden its dissemination.
After two years, Huìsōng was indeed able to obtain an ancient manuscript from Cáoxī to collate against it,
resulting in a three-fascicle edition.
All these words were clearly those of the Sixth Patriarch,
free from any further error or fabrication;
he therefore commissioned artisans to carve them into printing blocks to collect these excellent accounts.
Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Venerable Master Liang of Wufeng in Mingzhou, composed on the nineteenth day of the third month in the third year of the Zhìhé era.
Regarding the recorded sayings of Venerable Master Liang of Wufeng in Mingzhou: it began with Śākyamuni Buddha.
Apart from the scriptural teachings,
he transmitted it to his senior disciple, Daigushi, by means of the Great Samādhi;
yet, this was not unrelated to the scriptural teachings.
This is indeed what is elucidated by the scriptural teachings.
It is intended to authenticate all dharma-gates and to establish them definitively as the ultimate pinnacle of the wondrous enlightenment.
When Bodhidharma received the lineage from the Great Kaula clan,
it was transmitted to the lands of China after twenty-eight generations.
Within China, it was further propagated by the sixth patriarch at Caoxi.
In times past,
before the various patriarchs had become fully established in their teachings,
they still relied on the scriptures to instruct their students.
I did not immediately reveal the essential truth alone to them.
Later sages, having personally encountered their capacities and what was appropriate for them,
proceeded to use this directly to awaken people.
Therefore, when he spoke of human affairs, people no longer referred to the words of the scriptures.
Consequently, those throughout the world who adhered strictly to the literal texts were left bewildered;
they claimed that he had departed from the scriptures and established heterodox views to criticize them.
Alas! How could this be known as the sutra that uniquely accords with the principle of "changing and thereby attaining flexibility"?
Yet, scholars do not easily reach it;
having reached it, they find it difficult to sustain it; and having sustained it, they find it difficult to discern its full meaning.
It is like people who all paint dragons but have never once captured the true form of a real dragon.
Even when someone shows them a real dragon, the world does not believe it;
for those in the world who truly recognize a dragon are few.
In this world, who does not speak of the Way?
It is transmitted everywhere in profusion;
yet as for whether what is thus transmitted accords with reality or not—[it remains to be seen].
How could one possibly exhaustively grasp all that they have distinguished?
I have therefore long been concerned that their confusion of the true Way constitutes a great malady for students;
I only regret that I am too timid to proclaim it.
Now I see that my teacher, Master Liang of Wufeng, is indeed a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
I was all the more delighted by his words,
and Master Liang likewise rejoiced at meeting me.
He then produced his recorded sayings and showed them to me.
Upon reading them, I found much therein to be exceptionally profound and subtle—
truly what is called "skillfully transforming and penetrating" the teachings.
Master Liang received it from Chan Master Ciming Yuan;
Ciming transmitted it to Linji,
who was the successor to Dazhi and Daji.
This Master Liang was a teacher of Chan practitioners;
as for the beauty of his refined cultivation, which earned him great acclaim from both the local inhabitants and those from all quarters,
this need not be discussed further.
Preface to the *Wuling Ji* (Collection from Wuling). Venerable Master Huìyuǎn was renowned throughout the four quarters for his possession of the Way during the Tiānxī and Qiánxì eras.
His fame was so widespread that students from both near and far flocked to him.
Like water flowing copiously downward,
I heard of this in my youth and regretted not having known that person.
Later, while traveling in Wu, I obtained these words from the two masters Qin and Xian.
Observing his detailed exposition and orderly responses,
his speech was invariably refined and elegant,
never allowing vulgar or commonplace expressions to emerge.
Although he entered and emerged from the great sūtras and śāstras,
he also perused secular documents and the teachings of Laozi and Zhuang Zhou without hesitation,
occasionally investigating their underlying meanings and ultimate purports.
Yet the profound mysteries of the Buddha-dharma seem impossible to exhaust through mere intellect;
only by spiritualizing and illuminating them can one come close to grasping them.
When the Great Master Bodhidharma first arrived in China with the Buddha’s Mind-Seal,
he encountered the Emperor of the Liang dynasty, who was addicted to conditioned phenomena and failed to comprehend his words.
Consequently, Bodhidharma traveled north to Mount Song.
Facing a wall, he sat in silence for nine years;
the doubts of the Chinese people gradually dissipated,
and the Way of Bodhidharma was thus transmitted.
For this reason, when later generations transmit the accounts of eminent monks,
they establish what is transmitted through meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, scholars of later times, lacking far-reaching insight, often believe the words of these transmitters to be true.
This is also an extreme lack of reflection.
How could the Way of Bodhidharma be limited merely to meditative contemplation? Now, "chan" (dhyāna) means stillness;
"guan" (vipaśyanā) means observation.
The Sage instructs beginners to quiet their thoughts and contemplate the Way.
This is what was transmitted by Dharmatrāta to his eminent disciple Mahākāśyapa.
In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to transform others through the Eye of the True Dharma,
it could be initiated through words,
but it could not be reached through words.
Therefore, he charged Mahākāśyapa to transmit it through the mind-to-mind succession;
this is what is called the True Dharma.
It is from this that the Great Teaching emerged.
This is why the various sutras are so illuminating.
One who attains this,
though they may speak of it in ten thousand ways, remains consistent with its essence.
What he speaks has never been mixed with extraneous things.
Those who do not grasp this,
though they may maintain silence and hold fast to it, will fail.
That which they maintain has never failed to be deluded.
Now, the words of the Venerable Master may truly be called the attainment of the True Dharma.
How could mere meditative contemplation ever exhaustively describe it?
The Master comes from the third generation after Master Yunmen;
Master Yunmen comes from the eighth generation after Master Dajian (the Sixth Patriarch).
Alas! We have become increasingly distant from the Sage.
Students today are beset by doubt and error.
At that time, the Master had been no more than a hundred years removed from Great Master Yunmen.
Holding fast to the True Dharma alone, he gazed toward those worthy people;
with resolute determination, he led his students,
using the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to rectify their transmission.
Truly, if one attains stillness to cease this frantic wandering,
their virtue regarding the path of instruction will reach its ultimate fulfillment.
After his passing—
His disciples compiled his words and named the collection after the place where he resided,
calling it the "Wuling Collection" (Wulíng jí).
Preface on the Twentieth Day of the First Month of Winter in the Year of Renwu of the Qingli Era.
Preface to the Yuanzong Ji (Collection on the Original Source). Some call it the Zongyuan Ji. Master Qin of Xiangjun has gathered the teachings of a hundred schools of Chan learning.
I have explored and selected those statements that are most profound,
compiling them next into a single work,
beginning from Śākyamuni Tathāgata and extending down to Yunmen.

The disciples who assisted in the compilation numbered three hundred and thirty-three in all; their recorded sayings comprise six hundred and twenty entries, totaling more than eighteen thousand words.
Thus the book was completed.
I have inscribed this with my humble name and arranged it.
Its great purport is that one’s realization arises from not following words;
it is ordinary yet concise and subtle, never losing its fundamental principle.
He has indeed attained it.
Therefore, it is said that Yuanzong Qinshi realized the Dharma under Master Deshan Yuan and received formal certification from Master Sanjiao Cheng.
Both Cheng and Yuan were grand-disciples of the Great Master Yunmen Kuangzhen.
Yunmen received the Dharma from Chan Master Yunfeng Cun;
Yunfeng received it from Deshan Xuanjian.
Deshan continued the lineage of Longtan;
Longtan succeeded Tianhuang;
Tianhuang followed Master Shitou; and Shitou inherited from the Venerable Sengcan of Luling.
Master Si received the Dharma from the Sixth Patriarch, Zen Master Dajian;
he widely propagated the Way transmitted by Bodhidharma.
Consequently, those throughout the world who study Buddhism revere his virtue.
Just as Confucius inherited from the Duke of Zhou and revitalized the Way of Yao and Shun, the Sage brings forth its application; this is what is meant by "teaching.
Its great application cannot be fully exhausted in a single lifetime.
He took the written words themselves as the means for reaching [the truth].
Yet, as the various dharma-gates of the knowledge of all modes became ten thousandfold,
he further feared that those of great learning in future generations might fall into error.
Because those who study are unable to keep pace with the teachings,
Śākyamuni Tathāgata directly transmitted the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa;
although he manifested verbal explanations, he left no traces in written characters.
Bodhidharma departed twenty-nine generations after the Tathāgata;
having received the Dharma, he came to the East,
and at first people did not understand him.
At that time, [the teachings] were all cast aside; yet when they reached the era of the Great Mirror (Da Jian), they were widely believed.
Those who rushed to study them were like water flowing down with great force.
Alas! In this final age of the Semblance Dharma, we are increasingly distant from the Sage.
Scholars have engaged in forced interpretations and thereby lost the true Way;
thus, the Master Qin sighed deeply over them.
Therefore, he has rectified their ultimate tenets.
It is my hope that there may be something herein to correct.
This was on the day of the full moon in the first month of winter in the year Kangding Xinsi.
Preface to the Poem on Moving the Stone. Preface to the Poem on Moving the Stone. The poem on moving the stone is a tribute to the excellence of the gentleman who moved it.
When it was first cast aside by the roadside,
although it was magnificent, extraordinary, and grand enough to be admired,
passersby took no notice of it.
The Master Wubian contemplated this and sought to manifest it;
the artisans applied themselves with such diligence that it was completed in less than a morning,
and it was thus brought before his courtyard gate.
The rugged cliffs and hollowed-out voids rise like mountains, with caves and grottoes;
one gazes forward upon a clear pond while being sheltered behind by lush trees.
To the left and right, three halls were further opened up.
They were called Shiyán (Stone Banquet),
Zhàogǔ (Illuminating Antiquity),
and Chányàn (Chan Banquet).
Facing it caused people to feel a sense of leisurely, profound reflection.
From then on, those who boasted of it informed one another, and spectators flocked to view it;
thus, the beauty of the stone was suddenly made manifest.
Wubuian again composed a poem to sing of it;
worthy scholars and gentlemen, as well as those in monastic robes who were skilled in poetry,
also followed suit by composing verses.
Since you insist that I write a preface,
I shall comply; yet every person has matters they take pleasure in,
which may be refined or vulgar, licentious or upright.
By examining an object, one can know whether its maker is virtuous or not.
Take stone, for instance:
its nature is hard and its substance is firm.
Its form is still and its momentum is square.
That which is square seems like a gentleman who is strong and upright, yet not frivolous.
That which is still seems like a gentleman who does not act upon what is unrighteous.
"Solidity" seems like the nobleman who maintains his integrity without wavering;
"firmness" seems like the nobleman who is bold and incisive and able to stand firm.
Yet, the reputation of the "Shifting Stone" is even more admirable than these.
Its outer peaks and ridges seem like those of a worthy man, grave and solemn in his treatment of things;
its inner hollows seem like those of a perfected person, empty-minded and in harmony with the Dao.
Now, though lacking the eloquence to treat my Way as a teacher of Chan, I take up brush and ink to associate with Confucian scholars.
Having obtained this stone, I shall plant it in my courtyard so that I may gaze upon it morning and evening, desiring to draw sustenance from its six qualities.
I considered this to be an external incentive for moral cultivation and a silent witness to one's practice; yet,
upon reading his poetry...
If one seeks that which constitutes the intention [behind these teachings],
it has never failed to accord with this; yet,
no one has discerned that their minds are so far apart.
As for those worldly objects of empty play, they are certainly not worth comparing to this;
it is only fitting, therefore, that you gentlemen compose poems in praise of its beauty.
His poems number so-and-so many;
they are all the finest examples of poetry, such that their excellence is evident upon inspection.
How could my humble critique possibly evaluate them all in full?

In the month and day of such-and-such a year, during the [such-and-such] season, the monk Fayan composed a preface for his "Ten Poems on the Ten Verses. Regarding the "Ten Poems on the Ten Verses" by the monk Fayan:
the monk Zhoushan Fayan renovated the western wing of his residence and named it "Cuiyue Hall" (Hall of Verdant Foliage).
This was because he obtained the beautiful shade of the mountain forests.
He named the gate on its northern wall "Shizhai" (Ascending the Cliff),
to demonstrate that when ascending to heights, one must necessarily tread upon the path of rectitude.
The path by which one first enters the forest is called the Path of Whistling at the Moon;
it is so named because of the loftiness of the destination.
He cleared the spring and named it the Summer-Cool Spring.
I value his cleansing of the world from its feverish distress.
To commemorate the monk of old, I have named this stupa "Huayan" (Avataṃsaka);
it is because his virtue was equal to that of the person [of that name].
Pointing to the most precipitous peak of the ridge, he called it Qiaoge Ridge (Chanting Woodsmen's Song Ridge),
for he delighted in rustic affairs.
He named his pavilion Yingfa Pavilion (Pavilion of Radiant Illumination).
This is what Prince Wenxuan meant by "the mountains and rivers reflecting and enhancing one another.
He named the valley of this mountain Yuyin (Bathing Sound) and called it Yangmei U (Yangmei Grove),
distinguishing it for its superior fruits.
He inscribed the pavilion with the name "Qingyin Pavilion" (Pavilion of Pure Seclusion), because it could provide tranquility.
He cleared a space among the bamboos to create the "Xiuzhu Xuan" (Bamboo Cultivation Studio),
to emulate their upright character.
These ten verses refer to Fayun Monastery.
Fayun Monastery is situated within Daci Mountain, at a distance of approximately ten *li* from the city walls.
To the north it overlooks the Zhejiang River;
to the south it connects with the Qiantang Lake.
Crossing over successive ridges and layered peaks, one proceeds tranquilly along streams and wades through mountain torrents.
The sound of the water is clear and cold, and the clouds and trees are deep and misty;
compared to the mountains bordering rivers and lakes,
Mount Daci is the most secluded and profound.
The precincts of Fayun Temple are elegant and refined, while the surrounding forests and ridges coil in lush verdure.
Compared to other temples on Mount Ci,
this one stands out as truly exceptional.

he further announced, "Once the rites are completed, I shall await my orders at the palace gate.
At that time, the scholars of Qiantang admired him, as he possessed the reputation of one capable of holding office among the princes and nobles.
They deliberated together, saying,
"Fufeng is the land of Qin;
it is currently being agitated by the Rong and Di tribes."
"How could it be appropriate to go there?
It would be better for the Son of Heaven to send princes and lords to bestow grace upon our state.
Those who understand affairs criticized this, saying:
This is the nature of ordinary people;
it does not mean they recognize the worthy.
Now, kings and lords may be worthy and possess both capacity and discernment.
He delved into the Way of Wen and Wu through his studies;
he manifested a resolute spirit and established a great principle of conduct.
Just as the state was about to carry out a major judicial execution, he stepped forward.
Intending to eliminate the wicked and restore the orderly governance of a peaceful era,
one must surely exert oneself to demonstrate one's talents;
how could one be content to merely follow the crowd in evading hardships?
May you fortunately enjoy peace and security in this tranquil place.
Some say that the court has long subjected the princes and dukes to menial offices.
Furthermore, was it not because his worthiness had been recognized that he was to receive a prominent office?
In the midst of the intense heat of the year of Xinsi,
he indeed came from Xin-ding, intending to proceed toward the capital, and passed through Qiantang on his way.
Qianzi, following the intent of those who discussed the song,
composed another song, saying:
"The aspirations of the worthy and heroic..."
Free and unrestrained,
lofty and far-reaching—
how could the common world easily comprehend such a person?
Magnanimous and of great integrity,
he remained steadfast when faced with affairs;
he would rather maintain his integrity than let security ruin his reputation.
The gentleman feels shame at such conduct.
The heavens are vast and azure;
the palaces stand in tiered array.
The princes harbor lofty ambitions,
about to manifest the wonders within their breasts;
the Qin Sea is vast and boundless.
The trees along the Long Mountains stand in lingering sorrow;
as for the princes and lords who have departed,
they have resolved to leave and offer no protest.
Bestowing grace upon this single district,
you rouse the weariness of the people;
you shall likewise bestow virtue upon them.
At the frontier of the Qing and Qin,
when the miasmic vapors were cleared away,
the auspicious destiny grew ever more radiant.
Fame and achievement go hand in hand;
for a thousand years they shall flourish.
Preface to the Poem Sent Off Zhou Gan as He Enters the Capital Preface to the Poem Sent Off Zhou Gan as He Enters the Capital: Gan had resigned from office due to the mourning for his father.
He immediately rented a house in Qiantang and lived there for three years.
Although he lacked even a single *dan* or *shi* of grain in his stores, he remained as tranquil as ever.
He never once stepped through the gates of the powerful or wealthy to proclaim his poverty.
He engaged with his associates with sincerity rather than by virtue of their talent;
thus, from the scholar-officials down to the commoners of the villages,
both those who knew him and those who did not all esteemed him for his character.
However, this alone is not sufficient to constitute one who truly understands resonance.
Now, as for those who practice with self-confidence in their Way and do not frivolously debate with others—
such individuals, whether they encounter adversity or success, never overstep the bounds of their integrity and righteousness.
This, too, is simply the constant way of the gentleman.
It is likely that the vulgar and the impetuous are unable to maintain it;
thus, it is only natural that they attribute its excellence to external influence.
His benevolence and righteousness were innate;
through his reading and studies, his insight and discernment became clear and far-reaching.
He discoursed upon the rites, music, punishments, and governance of antiquity and the present.
When one points out what is right or wrong among them, there is nothing that is not correct.
If such a person were to attain their ambitions and govern a single province, a single district, or even the whole world and the state,
they would surely be able to provide benevolent administration and instruction to the people, ensuring that no one harbored resentment or longing.
How could it be that one is deemed worthy merely for self-reliance and steadfast poverty?
Between the recipient and the stimulus, their mutual understanding is the deepest;
I have often lamented my lack of power to promote it.
This spring, having completed the period of mourning for my father, I was again appointed to an official post in the capital.
You, Master Meng, were likewise about to return to Mount Lu.
Regrettably, our parting shall be far-reaching.
He composed a poem to dispel his lingering thoughts of attachment, saying:
"In wandering with you,
my heart grows ever more at ease."
Parting from you,
my heart grows anxious day by day;
for you are departing.
The spring waters flow surging and vast;
the azure heavens are ninefold,
and the cloud-palaces lie in misty obscurity.
Their aspirations for grandeur soar side by side; yet I,
cherishing virtue, advance alone.
Who among men would join me?
Rice is as precious as jade;
firewood is like the cassia branch.
Having stayed in the capital for nine years,
what was it that sustained me?
In the fifth month of Jiangnan—
The *yáo* grass grows by every fence;
return early, that you may comfort this longing.
Preface to the Poems Sent to Zhou Gongji. Preface to the Poems Sent to Zhou Gongji: In the past, Qianzi was in Xunyang.
When Gongji was still a youth, he became a student under my friend Zhou Shuzhi;
he was dedicated to his studies, profound and composed,
and never spoke without due reflection.
He was utterly unlike other students.
Qianzi once said to Shuzhi,
"The scenery and atmosphere of the rivers and mountains of Xunyang are pure and refined."
It is fitting that this should be concentrated in such a person; among these students,
it seems that Zhou’s son has attained it.
I observed that his studies had achieved fruition;
more than ten years after Qianzi left Xunyang,
I indeed heard that Gongji had passed the jinshi examinations and attained the rank of scholar-official.
Subsequently, it was heard that he had been appointed as the Magistrate of Jiande following a recommendation by the worthy Provincial Inspector, Master Li;
before a single year had passed, his reputation as a virtuous magistrate spread throughout the land.
Last autumn, I came to Hangzhou on business and stayed temporarily in Qiantang,
where I was able to travel back and forth among the mountains and observe his governance of the people.
In his youth he was skilled in administrative arts, yet he frequently employed benevolence and righteousness.
He was reverent and diligent in attending to affairs; his conduct was upright and his integrity incorruptible.
In his relations with others, he grew increasingly respectful as time passed.
Before a month had passed, the people of Hangzhou unanimously praised him.
Qianzi felt secretly delighted, thinking,
"I am fortunate that my previous words have been proven true."
Yet, he was called a man of superior wisdom and a gentleman of the Way.
Throughout his life, he most delighted in advancing others through benevolence and righteousness and in exhorting the transformation of social customs.
It is regrettable that he died young, so that we do not see the public achievements he would have established had he lived on.
Although Gongji came to provide me with resources for my own self-cultivation,
how could I have known that this unworthy one would rely upon the assistance provided by his virtuous teacher and skillful guidance?
It was only when I met Qianzi that I first resolved to devote myself to the transmission of the Way.
My grievances have not yet been fully set forth;
may you, sir, rectify this injustice and exert your strength to vindicate me.
Such sincerity and diligence would not have been surpassed even by the most resolute scholars of antiquity.
As he was about to depart, [the Master] felt deeply moved by his intention;
he then composed a poem to see him off.
The poem says:
A refined spirit broods within this man’s person.
When I beheld him in the past, he stood preeminent and unlike all others;
now, examining his record of governance, it shines forth with brilliant clarity.
Alas for my teacher, who shall no longer behold the wind of the superior man.
Now that we part at the river’s edge,
I hasten toward the twin palace gates from a thousand li away.
The imperial throne is resplendent, yet the gates of the sovereign are solemn and deep.
Strive to advance yourself; do not allow yourself to sink into obscurity.

Preface to the Farewell of Secretariat Zhou Gan as He Returns South From Hangzhou to Jiangnan and Guangzhou, traveling by land through the southern regions, the postal stations span five or six thousand *li*.
By turning toward the great ocean, one obtains a ship driven by the gale;
it travels a thousand li in a single day.
Otherwise, one remains on other islands for many months and years.
Therefore, when people from the south came to Wu,
they always regarded this as a hardship.
Now that I have been a guest in Qiantang for two springs already, those coming from the south are few and far between.
In the third month of the Gengchen year,
a guest informed me on behalf of the Zhou Commandant, saying:
"The Commandant is a native of Feng."
"Why do you not go see him?
One day I went to his gate and happened upon him as he was coming out.
I returned home feeling dejected and somewhat ill at ease.
After several days had passed, the Commandant indeed arrived at my residence with his mounted attendants;
he entered my room and spoke with me.
The affairs of his native village were vividly illuminated before his ears and eyes;
he spoke of his past life as if to an old friend,
speaking with such earnestness that he could not cease.
His breast and mind were expansive and open;
one could see that he was a man of great character.
At dusk, he took his leave.
I was struck by this as extraordinary and said to those who understand such matters:
"The Commandant has exerted himself with his literary compositions and sworn oaths."
It was not that he would refuse office because it was not obtained through the jinshi examination.
He had been unsuccessful before the authorities on four occasions, yet he never altered his resolve.
When he finally attained it, he did not decline the sovereign's command on the grounds that the post was too distant from his home.
From the capital, as if from his own hometown,
he welcomed his parents to Qiantang;
the journey was nearly ten thousand li.
One should not consider it a hardship because one's salary is meager or that one lacks sufficient strength.
When serving in office, if one is excessively frugal, one will even desire to buy water.
Truly, the scholar’s only concern is the lack of integrity.
One need not worry about failing to establish oneself;
however, if one faces affairs in the morning and loses what they maintain by evening,
they will have no leisure for forced smiles or sycophancy to accommodate others.
When there was benefit to be gained, they contended;
when there was no benefit, they withdrew.
Before even a hundred li from their home villages had passed, [they were already at odds].
Thus, throughout the day he remains dissatisfied and behaves like a child;
how then could one expect his great fame to leave such brilliant traces as to illuminate the world and posterity like that of Wei?
To maintain one's integrity and conduct with consistency from beginning to end—
is this not truly the spirit of a noble and magnanimous man?
I have heard an ancient tradition say:
In the south, where there is pure yang, those who obtain its proper qi will necessarily be firm,
vigorous, balanced, and upright, as well as intelligent and wise.
Among my subordinates, all are people from the south.
Alone, I am timid, dull-witted, and lacking even a single virtue with which to administer medicine to my own nature;
yet I am further unable to cast it off with lofty detachment and roam expansively with all things through this world.
Do you not feel that you ought not to bring shame upon those who gave you birth?
It is precisely through this that one expresses the sentiments of one's native land;
how could it be as Zhuang Zhou said—that the further one goes from others, the more distant one becomes?

Thus, my thoughts for this man grow ever deeper. Preface to the Parting of the Scholar Lin Yefu as He Returns to Chaoyang The world says that Chaoyang abounds in gentlemen. It is said that there are many virtuous men in this region. Now, the scholar Lin Yefu has returned to his home in Chaoyang; I have composed this preface to bid him farewell. As for the origins of the name "Chaoyang," it is recorded in the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian) that during the reign of Emperor Gaozu of Han, when the imperial army was stationed at Chang'an, the people of the south were summoned to provide corvée labor. Among them was a man named Chen Sheng, who was skilled in the art of divination. He observed the celestial omens and declared, "The auspicious signs point toward the Yangzi River. Consequently, he led his followers to settle in the marshlands along the Yangzi. Because the land was situated between the Chaoshan and the Yangzhou, it was named "Chaoyang. Over the course of generations, the descendants of these settlers have flourished and produced many eminent figures. Although the region is remote from the central plains, its people have long been renowned for their integrity and learning. This is why the world speaks of the abundance of gentlemen in Chaoyang. Now, the scholar Lin Yefu is one such person. His ancestors were of noble lineage, and he himself possesses refined character and extensive knowledge. Having served at court, he has now retired to his native place to care for his aged parents. His conduct is upright and his reputation is high. To part from such a man is indeed a cause for deep reflection. I have therefore written this preface to express my sentiments as he departs for his hometown. May his journey be safe and may he find joy in his native land. Preface to the Parting of the Scholar Lin Yefu as He Returns to Chaoyang. The world says that Chaoyang abounds in gentlemen. Yet the Lin clan was the most flourishing.
When I first visited my late father, the Magistrate of Fields (Tiancao) Yefu, in Hangzhou,
I observed his broad-mindedness, clarity, and pure integrity.
He exerted himself in practicing the ancient Way in his governance;
he was not narrow-minded or pedantic in his administrative affairs.
Thus, one can truly say that those who praise him do so not falsely.
Later, when they met in Fanyang,
Lu Yuanbo said to Yefu Zhongfu,
"Master Xun was one who knew [the Way] from birth."
He studied the Six Classics and explored the works of the hundred schools,
being able to fathom their depths and investigate them thoroughly;
he came close to the Way of the Sages.
He stood out preeminently, having attained self-realization.
He considered that the *Yi* exhausts the Way of the Three Poles;
it is the treasury of the sages.
I alone lament that although Master Yang Xiong wished to clarify it,
his understanding of the Mysterious (xuan) had not yet reached its ultimate depth;
thus, he composed the *Caofan*.
He intended thereby to clarify the beginning and end of the Way of the *Yi*.
Furthermore, asserting that ritual and music are of primary importance for one who would establish a dynasty,
he also composed the *Liyue* (Book of Ritual and Music).
This is to demonstrate the beginning of the sovereign’s governance;
fundamentally, it shows that the Confucian is not anxious for wealth and honor,
but rather possesses lofty integrity and transcends the mundane.
In emulating the moral teachings of the ancient sages and worthies,
I further believe that the prosperity of the Lin clan has a profound basis.
At this time, having completed his term as Director of the Ministry of Agriculture, he was about to proceed to the imperial court.
Yuanbo returned south, while I traveled east to Kuaiji.
Two years later,
I came back to Hangzhou once more.
Furthermore, I heard that Tian Cao was bedridden with illness in the capital.
When his condition reached the point of imminent death,
this rustic man indeed supported him on a litter and returned to bury him in his ancestral land.
He had come by boat from Wujiang;
I went to offer my condolences to him on another day.
Both the elder and younger brothers, the "wild men," were sorrowful and emaciated.
He was nearly unable to bear his grief.
When the time for the ritual of taking the precepts arrived, he said to me,
"Why do you not compose a song to bid me farewell as I return?"
I have reflected that the Lin clan is the most prominent in Chaoyang.
Since song cannot fully express their excellence as prose can, I shall set it forth in ci.
I have heard that Heaven produces sages.
Therefore, they act on behalf of Heaven’s work,
assisting in the Way of Heaven and Earth.
It is fitting that such worthy ones should enjoy long life and be prominent in their positions.
Thus, Yan Yuan died young and Bo Niu suffered from illness;
Mencius encountered misfortune, while Xun Qing and Yang Xiong were left despondent in their time;
and figures such as Jia Yi and Dong Zhongshu, though appearing in succession, met with untimely misfortunes.
I do not know what the one who directs all things intends by this.
For instance, the benevolence of Tiacao of Nan’an and the wisdom and insight of his younger brother were both eminent;
yet before they had fully exercised their great talents, they both passed away prematurely at the age of twenty.
Even among those of clear wisdom who hear this, who would not be perplexed?
Some might say that Mr. Lin’s longevity does not reside in his own person, but rather in his descendants.
I heard that a rustic man took flesh from his own thigh with a blade to heal his father;
though he desired his father’s illness to be cured, it ultimately did not accord with his wishes.
The gentleman called him one of pure filial piety.
If this rustic man can lead his elder and younger brothers to practice the benevolence and filial piety of Tian Cao and pursue the learning of Master Xun,
then the longevity of our clan will surely find its locus therein; its sincerity and brilliance will grow ever greater for future generations.
Yuanbo was also a man of the Way.
He was a relative by marriage to the commoners;
had he merely collaborated with them to cultivate fame and integrity, the prosperity and excellence of the Lin family would have been preserved.
How could it merely illuminate Chaoyang and the present day?
It shall surely radiate its brilliance throughout all future generations and across the world.

Preface to the Song Sent Off Master Fanci Ji upon His Return to Tiantai: Now, those who are Buddhists cultivate the Way that transcends the world; they maintain themselves in purity and do not associate with the secular.
Since he did not employ his teachings and path to push his way through the world or merely to exhort others,
how could it be appropriate for him to pursue worldly affairs and wander among the mundane?
This was the Great Master Fancai.
In his youth, he was celebrated for his poetry in the capital;
later, upon returning to Tiantai, he applied himself even more diligently to our Way.
One day, he conceived the idea of using Buddhist matters to exhort the class of scholar-officials.
Last year, when I traveled through the regions of Western Zhejiang and the Huai plain,
all the high officials with reputations among the people were delighted to follow my cause.
They number no fewer than a hundred.
Were it not for sincere devotion and earnest resolve that exalt the Sage’s true teaching and its subtle Way,
how could such a great multitude of benevolent and virtuous gentlemen be obtained?
Alas! When people enter and exit the doors of the powerful and influential,
or hasten along the paths of power and profit,
their virtue cannot inspire the trust of others.
They were filled with doubt yet offered no explanation;
they were ruined by it yet failed to discern the truth.
With hollow cries and deceitful guile, they treated the Buddha as a mere object of mockery.
Fortuitously relying on outward appearances and borrowing from the momentum of circumstances to seek mere personal gain,
they rush toward death without regard for the teachings; such people have heard of the Master’s reputation.
"What should one take as the mind?
I admire what Master Ji has done;
therefore, I sing this song to bid him farewell on his return."
The song says:
When a person comes,
the worthy and eminent shall welcome them.
As the people returned,
their great undertaking was successfully completed;
the spring colors were exquisite and the spring breeze was light.
With sleeves grasping the clouds, I hasten on my distant journey;
Mount Tai rises above the void,
its atmosphere serene and pure.
One should truly appreciate what is appropriate and find rest in it;
do not look back upon floating fame.
As for those who pursue profit and forget the Way—
As for the prevailing customs and contemporary sentiments,
since they have perished along with our own school of thought,
what is there worth evaluating?
Preface to the Farewell of Dharma Master Zhen upon His Return to Mount Lu Five years have passed since I left Xunyang, and Dharma Master Zhen came from Mount Lu to meet me in Qiantang.
Upon hearing that he had first arrived, they were both joyful and astonished.
The Master, however, paid no heed to what the Prime Minister had obtained;
he shook out his robes and departed for Mount Hao.
"I vowed that for the rest of my life I would not set foot in the mundane world;
why then have you come here? When they conversed with one another, [he explained].
Only then did I realize that his plan for the Buddhist stupa was not undertaken as an ordinary matter, but rather because he had shifted his will toward it.
While I was in Xunyang, I once discussed the characters of men with Zhou Shuzhi.
Because the Master was pure and capable of instructing students through his Way,
Shuzhi often commended him with words of high praise.
Consequently, I, along with Guo Shubao and Pei Changyan, frequently visited his door.
They took turns composing songs and poems to extol his virtues;
the Master also joyfully recognized his excellence.
Now he has traveled thousands of li from here.
I met with him again, and before half a year had passed,
his words became increasingly refined and his Way increasingly intimate;
our bond of mutual understanding and sincerity grew a hundredfold thicker than it was at first.
In the eighth month of autumn, the True Master gathered those with whom he had planned his affairs and ordered the boats to set sail.
The people of Hangzhou, filled with reverence and admiration, bowed their heads and entreated him most earnestly to remain.
In the end, he also departed and did not look back.
I traveled through the four quarters alone to Xunyang;
I felt a lingering attachment as if I were longing for my parents' homeland, unable to forget it.

This is because there are benevolent and virtuous gentlemen therein who are earnest, substantial, sincere, and trustworthy in their social relations, employing the Way and its Virtue to mutually nourish one another;
furthermore, Mount Kuanglu anchors its left flank, its jagged peaks rising loftily and its atmosphere appearing profoundly deep and secluded.
He caused others to study it so that they might develop ambitions that transcend the world.
Now that the true master has returned there,
I am constrained by circumstances and cannot go with him.
My vast and boundless thoughts have become increasingly turbulent within my breast.
Therefore, I ask you, Master, to convey my thanks to the gentlemen of Xunyang:
whether in poverty or success, in honor or decline, it is these things that weary my physical form.
To scheme over gain and loss in their myriad forms exhausts my mind.
Human life is but like a single dream;
why should I long remain enmeshed with things within this world?
It is fitting that you should explore the Buddha-way deeply and purify your spiritual intelligence.
Since a true master is one who leads others on the Path,
it would be appropriate to command him to travel with you.

9. Epigraphic Titles for Records and Inscriptions (12). Record and Inscription Title:
*Wulin shan zhi*. This mountain extends to the northwest of Hangzhou;
its paths enter from the north and south, flanking the lake.
To the south, one exits the western gate, turns toward Mount Chì, crosses Mài Ridge,
and passes through Yānzhī. To the north,
one exits Qiántáng Gate and ascends the "Stone of the First Emperor’s Mooring Cable."
Passing the Qinwang and Qingting mountains,
I descended until reaching the foot of Tuohan Ridge, where I turned left,
entered Yuan Gong’s Pine Gate, and arrived at Xingchun Bridge.
This is a branch road leading south from the western side of the bridge.
After traveling two li past Xingchun Bridge,
one reaches the junction where the north-south roads meet.
There is a small inn with residents where travelers may rest.
Proceeding further west for two li.
Entering the gates of the two monasteries,
one passes by Hejian Bridge and Longji Bridge; from there,
one proceeds to Danxia and Ziwai Pavilion.
