The Venerable Gaoshi opened the southern wing of his hermitage, fully capturing the scenic beauty of the mountains and rivers, which is so vivid it seems one could wash oneself within its sight.
Su Zimei of Wugong first named it "The Clear Pavilion.
Subsequently, many virtuous scholars and gentlemen visited it for pleasure and composed verses in its praise.
The Elder [Dafu] then followed their intent.
He then ordered Qianzi to compose an inscription for it.
Since Qianzi could not decline the request,
he said to the Master:
Among heaven, earth, and the myriad things, there are none that do not possess both the pure and the turbid.
Their manifestations are all capable of moving people, leading them toward either order or chaos.
Now, when the purity of heaven and earth moves people, it does so with solemnity.
The purity of the sages and worthies moves people with solemnity;
the purity of the times moves people with refinement;
the purity of mountains and rivers moves people with freshness.
As for Heaven and Earth acting as the clear transformative agency of time and the world,
I cannot attempt to deliberate upon or describe them.
As for the clarity of the sages, the worthies, and the mountains and rivers—
This can be extended by inference to benefit the world.
The Venerable Shangren opened this pavilion,
bringing together the stillness of the mountain and the clarity of the water.
One who awaits those who come and rewards them finds their mind opened and their spirit refreshed;
their thoughts and deliberations no longer wander into excess or stagnation.
This also benefits many people.

Some find it opens and clarifies their minds, leading them to contemplate returning to the ultimate purity and supreme stillness; others say that to roam at ease within supreme stillness is to fully realize the intent of the chariot. Thus, its purpose is all the more attained.
Qianzi thereupon inscribed this, saying:
"The myriad phenomena of heaven and earth are both turbid and clear."
When purity moves others,
people become upright;
when turbidity moves others, they become corrupt.
When humanity falls into chaos,
one must be pure and upright;
thus, cultivate your virtue with diligence.
In turbidity and disorder,
your wickedness flourishes.
Be vigilant, O gentleman!
Choose the times that are appropriate;
O noble person, observe the precepts!
Be cautious regarding what you indulge in during those times.
Your carriage is indeed bright;
your radiance is indeed pure.
There are mountains, lofty and high.
Therein one may unburden the emotions.
There are waters, clear and sparkling,
wherein one may wash the ceremonial cap-strings.
Having purified one's will,
having clarified one's spirit;
being pure and clean in thought and deed.
This is indeed the ultimate fulfillment;
do not disparage it as being like a mere carriage-porch.
Let this be a source of sublime appreciation.
Do not say these are external objects;
they are the rewards of the divine.
Be pure and lofty.
It is only that which the Way employs;
one must be diligent in this intent.

That "Superior Man" (shangren) does not have his name recorded in the original collection, which is suspicious; it is likely that those of high discernment merely attributed their own sentiments to him.
Inscription for Nanxuan (The Southern Gabled Hall), with Preface Nanxuan lies directly north of Nanping Mountain.
The mountain is only a few hundred paces away;
one can lean against the gabled hall and gaze upon it.
Grass, trees, clouds, and objects—not even a hair’s breadth was hidden.
When the rain cleared, the mountain light shone forth with such clarity that it illuminated the pillows and mats.
In summer, the auspicious breeze wafted gently, arriving of its own accord without being sought.
In winter, one properly embraces the great sun; it blazes and shines, yet sometimes it follows the piercing cold and harshness.
There was a guest who was leisurely and relaxed, having no use for the world, and was able to spend his whole day looking up and down amidst this scene.
Often his robes were spread wide and his spirit was vast and majestic,
as if standing alone beyond heaven and earth. Indeed,
such was the profound observer of antiquity.
Who does not value attaining what is appropriate for one's affairs?
If it can rectify one's thoughts so that good fortune, misfortune, regret, or shame do not harm the Way,
then even a thatched cottage with earthen steps is not considered humble.
Tao Yuanming said:
"I sigh and swagger beneath the eastern window,
contentedly passing through this life."
Is this not indeed finding one’s proper destination?
Nanxuan is the rear chamber of my lodgings;
Master Wei did not begrudge this unworthy man his quarters here.
When the occasion arose for me to depart, I thought of Nanxuan, who—possessing complete simplicity and folly—seemed to have found his proper place.
Even though his host employed him with various tasks, he still hurried to obey orders;
how much more so when he was honored by being received with virtue and righteousness?
Furthermore, how could one lightly depart from Nanxuan?
The inscription says:
Looking back at Nanxuan—what is he doing? He stands there, looking up and down, hesitating and lingering.
I give voice to that beauty;
it accords with my own simplicity.
I and Nanxuan are like two halves of a whole.
Inscription on the Old Inkstone, with Preface:
When I was in my hometown, my late friend, the Daoist Master Ma Zhizhang, presented me with an inkstone from Duankui as a gift.
As I traveled to various regions, the inkstone accompanied me everywhere.
It has now been fourteen years since Zhi Zhang unfortunately died young. Alas!
Zhi Zhang was a man of integrity and trustworthiness.
He was fond of learning and possessed a resolute purity,
striving to maintain lofty principles.
Though he failed to fulfill his aspirations, Heaven snatched away his life before his time.
Whenever I looked at this inkstone, I would often find myself thinking of that man;
thus, I have kept it and never once cast it aside.
This was the final winter month of the first year of the Kangding era.
For it, an inscription was made,
saying: "If such a person passes away,
our spiritual communion comes to an end."
With a heart as firm as metal and stone, regard this as a treasure.
Inscribed on the wall of the Lotus Fragrance Pavilion of Master Quan of Qiantang West Lake. The atmosphere of West Lake is not like that of any other place.
The morning glow and evening mists are alternately dark and translucent;
there is no time when they are not beautiful.
Mountain ridges and pavilions shimmer with intermingled gold and emerald hues.
Lotus flowers battled the wind, their fragrance dispersing in all directions;
as one gazed upon this pervasive scent, it was as if one had suddenly entered a wondrous realm.
Yet, such is the way the clarity or turbidity of the human heart responds to external objects.
Thus, how could one who pursues the Way not choose their dwelling?
The Venerable Quan recited the sutras and composed poetry,
practiced the "cursive holy" script, and renovated the Lotus Fragrance Pavilion.
Appreciating the scenery of Lake Zi helps to purify the mind;
thus, the flourishing interest in the Way may be clearly seen.
Written on the twenty-fifth day of the final month of winter in the Jiyou year of the Xining era by Qianzi.
The Monument to Wénzhōngzǐ: "The goodness of the world resides in the Way of the Sage;
furthermore, the principles of the world reside in the talent of the Sage."
To possess talent but not the Way means that instruction does not reach transformation.
To possess the Way but not talent [is likewise incomplete].
Transformation does not reach where teaching does.
Yao and Shun were those who attained the Way of the sages;
Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and the Duke of Zhou were those who attained the talent of the sages.
One who attains both of these is the sage, Confucius, also known as Zhongni.
Therefore it is said:
"The Master was far superior to Yao and Shun."
More than a hundred years after the death of Zhongni (Confucius), Mencius appeared;
though he did not equal Zhongni, he was one who opened the way for him.
After Mencius’s death, Xun Qingzi appeared.
After Xun Qing passed away, Yangzi Yun succeeded him.
Both Xun and Yang were those who extolled Zhongni;
yet their teachings were specialized and their doctrines were not uniform.
Mengzi was next [in rank].
More than a thousand years after Confucius, he was born during the period between the Chen and Sui dynasties and was styled Wenzhongzi (Master of Literature).
At first, he used the twelve strategies to probe the will of the ruler of the time;
seeing that he could not be worked with,
he rolled them up and tucked them away.
He returned to Fenzhou in the north and greatly revitalized his teachings;
as soon as the thunder rolled, the four seas sought out its sound,
and three thousand disciples came to him.
He was one who resembled Zhongni.
At that time, the Way had been lost throughout the world,
and the feudal lords, high ministers, and great officers were unable to cultivate it.
In his writings alone, Wenzhongzi consistently acted according to ritual propriety, striving to rectify men and rescue all beings.
He once said:
"When the Way prevails in the world, the sage hides within it."
When the Way is absent from the world, the sage manifests his sageliness;
yet returning to the One leaves no trace—is this not concealment?
By relying on the Two to achieve salvation, how could there be no manifestation?
In the past, the governance of the Two Emperors and Three Kings was upright yet unrecorded;
the governance of the feudal lords and Five Hegemons was lost yet undiscriminated.
Confucius gave literary form to these matters as the Six Classics, thereby providing a complete system of instruction and transformation for posterity.
Later, when the two Han dynasties possessed the empire,
they employed a mixture of the systems of King Wen and Duke Huan;
it was rare that their governance reached the standard of true rectitude.

From the Three Kingdoms of Wei through to the Northern and Southern Dynasties, the ways of humanity were in utter chaos, and the ultimate standard was lost—some versions read "the ultimate character" (ji-zi). What has passed cannot be pursued; what is yet to come can still be regulated.
The Way of the former kings was flourishing and about to be eclipsed by the earth.
Wenzhongzi lamented that later generations would have no law,
and he said:
For those who have studied the governance of Zhongni since the past millennium,
I cannot but concede my place to them; indeed,
I have drawn upon the administrations of the Han, Wei, and the Six Dynasties.
As for Wen’s continuation of the Classics,
it was intended to broaden the edification of future generations.
Were it not for the Way of a sage and the talent of a sage, who else could have been capable of such a task?
Wen-zhong was to Zhongni as the sun is to the moon.
When the Tang dynasty arose, his disciples obtained the classics of Wen-zhong and used them to govern the world.
The world eventually reached a state of rectitude;
rites, music, and institutions shone with brilliance.
For four hundred years, it rivaled the glory of the Three Dynasties.
Alas! It has been nearly a hundred years since Zhongni passed away.
His teachings were brought to ruin by the Qin dynasty.
Among his disciples, those who followed his teachings and entered government service—
Yet, while [Wang Chong] was but a subordinate official of a regional state,
the disciples of Wenzhongzi were about to serve as ministers to the Son of Heaven;
thus, his teachings have spread to the present day.
How magnificent!
That he displays such lofty aspirations and far-reaching strides!
Could it be that Heaven has lent the virtue of Zhongni to Wenzhongzi?
I could not know it myself; however,
upon reading the genealogy of the Wang clan,
I appreciated what was found within its writings.
How great it is!
Thus the stele says: "Since the Six Classics, the Way of Governance has not been refined."
The great human relations are vast and expansive;
through expedient means, the practice of the orange tree flourishes.
Within the patterns of the written word, they are manifested.
The turbulent waves were clarified and the Six Classics were continued;
thus the world was transformed and perfected.
Confucius is like the sun;
his writings illuminate both worlds,
pervading ten thousand generations.
None can be compared to him.
A Detailed Record of the Deeds of the Late Great Dharma Master Ciyun Shi of Tiantong Temple in Wulin, Hangzhou. The Dharma Master’s name was Zunshe; his courtesy name was Zhibai.
His original surname was Ye,
and he was a native of Ninghai County in Linhai Prefecture.
Initially, his mother, Lady Wang, sought spiritual protection from the ancient Guanyin Bodhisattva, praying for a son.
One night, she dreamed that her chamber was bright and pure, and a beautiful woman appeared and gave her a luminous pearl to swallow.
When the Dharma Master was born at seven months of age,
he was already able to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara after his mother.
When he grew slightly older, he took no pleasure in following his elder brother in trade.
He subsequently went in secret to Dongye to become a monk under Master Yiquan.
One night prior to this, Yiquan had dreamed that a young boy was standing to the left of the Buddha statue in the temple.
The next day, the Dharma Master arrived;
his dream was thus verified.
He shaved off his hair at eighteen.
At the age of twenty, he received full ordination at Zenrin-ji Temple.
The following year, he studied the Vinaya under the Vinaya Master Shūsho.
At that time, the local school of the Tiantai tradition was flourishing greatly.
The students, admiring the Master’s brilliance and vigor,
repeatedly challenged him with poems to demonstrate their mastery of Confucian studies;
the Master immediately composed verses in response.
The poem says in brief:
"Ultimate emptiness is the field of selection;
Great Enlightenment is the official rank."
Having entered the country, he burned off a finger before the image of Samantabhadra at Guoqing Temple,
vowing to study the teachings of Tiantai.
He then gradually took up his book-bag and proceeded to the lecture hall of Master Yitong of Baoyun Temple.
While on the road, he dreamed of an old monk who said of himself, "I am Master Mañjuśrī.
Upon meeting Dōgen, he realized that the monk in his dream was indeed this very person.
He immediately took the teachings to heart and studied under him facing north.
Before long, he had mastered all that was transmitted by the Tiantai school,
including its subtle words and profound principles.
His wisdom and understanding were preeminent among his peers.
On the day his ancestral teacher, Zhizhe, entered parinirvāṇa,
he vowed to exert himself with all his might throughout the entire day, finally setting fire to the crown of his head.
He practiced the samādhi of the four dhyānas and, out of sincerity, composed verses to express his devotion; all such poems and stanzas are found in his collected works.
These details have been omitted here for brevity. After Master Tong had passed away, the Dharma Master immediately returned to Tiantai.
Due to his arduous studies, he once fell ill and vomited blood;
believing himself certain to die,
he resolutely entered the Buddha chamber at Lingxu.
He employed the incantation for subjugation and cursed him, saying:
"If the four teachings flourish and spread, then my illness shall be cured;
otherwise, I pray that I may end my life here."
On the evening of the twenty-first day, he suddenly heard a voice calling out from the air,
saying, "Zunshi will soon die.
The Dharma Master redoubled his efforts and remained undaunted.
On the thirty-fifth day, he suddenly saw corpses filling the room;
the Dharma Master was not confused and walked upon them to perform his practice,
whereupon the corpses immediately vanished.
When the repentance was completed on the forty-ninth day,
a voice was heard from the air, saying:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions increase your merit and longevity."
That evening, while he was in a state of deep sleep, he had a vivid vision of a giant holding a vajra and pointing it at his mouth.
Startled, he woke up, and his illness was immediately cured;
his eloquence flourished even further, and his voice, countenance, and spirit became more radiant than they had been in ordinary times.
The Dharma Master was deeply moved by its benefits and desired to engage in this practice;
he subsequently composed a work titled *The Liturgy for Paying Homage to Avalokiteśvara*.
Just as he was about to inscribe the title, a strange monk suddenly appeared and left behind a manuscript whose calligraphy and personal style were nearly identical to his own original draft.
At the beginning of the Chunhua era, the Dharma Master was twenty-eight years of age.
The assembly continued to reside at their master’s Baoyun lecture hall,
where he expounded upon the *Catuḥpariṣat-sūtra*. After many years,

while he was lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, and *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* sūtras, one day a mule from the Shi family came galloping and prostrated itself beneath his seat.
If there were those with the intent to listen,
they arrived at regular intervals for a total of forty days;
it ceased only after she gave birth.
That a donkey fruit possesses the intent of a human—
how strange this is!
It was in the year of Zidou (Cibin) of the Zhizhi era.
The Dharma Master, having gathered a congregation of both monastics and laypeople who were faithful,
studied the practices of the Pure Land according to the sutras and authored a work titled *Record of the Vow to Be Born in the Western Land*.
Furthermore, he modeled his practice on Samantabhadra’s benefit for others as the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).
Master Chu Baoyun remained there for another twelve years;
during this time, he never once went out to visit or socialize with worldly people.
Fortuitously, I received the command to assist in the creation of a statue of Great Compassion; the artisan fashioned it from sandalwood,
and once completed, I wore the image upon my head.
Yi further composed the text of the Fourteen Great Vows.
Later, when a craftsman mistakenly broke the willow branch held by the image,
the Dharma Master was filled with reverence and trepidation.
He immediately received it himself;
without relying on any adhesive, it joined seamlessly as before.
In the third year of the Xianping era, the region of Siming suffered a great drought.
The people of the commandery relied upon that rain;
the Dharma Master, however, had made a secret covenant through the invocation of the Avalokiteśvara Samādhi:
"If it does not rain within three days..."
He intended to immolate himself by fire.
As expected, rain fell throughout the commandery,
causing the Governor to regard it as a marvel.
He then inscribed these events upon a stele.
In the fifth year of the Xianping era, the Dharma Master returned once more to Tiantai;
though he wished to retreat to the east to live in seclusion, his followers became increasingly numerous.
He then immediately expanded the Xiyang Yihong Monastery and,
based on the scriptures, commissioned a great image of Amitābha Buddha.
They led one another in the practice of the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
He established the doctrine of practicing for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Regarding the lewd verses that had previously existed in his village, he rectified them all by consulting ancient laws;
furthermore, those who partook in improper sacrificial offerings were expelled.
As for what is called the White Crane Temple,
the people held it in especially high esteem and vied with one another to offer sacrifices with livestock.
The Dharma Master then exhorted the man to change his blood-offerings for vegetarian fasts.
When he and the multitude set out by boat for Baitiao, a violent storm suddenly arose;
the crowd believed this was the doing of the deity.
The Dharma Master then explained to the deity at the shrine the reasons for the Buddha’s prohibition against killing;
immediately, the waves subsided.
He then commanded the deity to receive the Buddha’s precepts.
Thereafter, sacrifices involving living animals were finally discontinued.
He then composed the "Record of the Wilderness Temple" (Yemiao Zhi) and entered into a covenant with the deity;
the people have followed this practice down to the present day.
In the fourth year of the Xiangfu era, when Lord Zhang Xun was serving as a provincial governor while holding the rank of Langguan, he encountered the three-year mourning period for his mother.
He subsequently appointed the Sangha Rectifier, Master Yan, to enter Jingde Vihāra in that prefecture to lecture on the *Mahā-śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation).
When the summer retreat had concluded,
three śramaṇas wearing patched robes arrived without any apparent cause and requested to join the *Ullambana* lecture assembly.
Just as he bowed and was about to sit, the figure suddenly vanished.
Once, while traveling elsewhere on an auspicious occasion, the Dharma Master passed through Huangyan;
a pig came running, circled the vehicle he was riding in, and then lay down before him.
If his mind had any desire,
the multitude would sigh in wonder, unable to fathom why; yet upon careful investigation,
it was found that he was merely a pig coming from the slaughterhouse to avoid being killed.
He then paid its price and instructed the butcher to release it,
ordering that it be raised at Miaoxi Temple.
It is called "Meeting with Goodness.
Now, as for the boar actually enjoying such virtue—how could that be?
On my estate, there is a temple called Chishan-ji.
It was high and cool, bordering the sea.
The Dharma Master once said to others,
"A stupa should be built here."
The local people there, all of whom delighted in hearing this, said:
"On the summit of this mountain, there is always a wondrous light that shines upon the sea;
within that light, the shadow of a seven-storied pagoda becomes increasingly visible."
However, the area reached by its illumination extended for forty *li*,
all of which was surrounded by the fishing nets of the fishermen.
Knowing that this emission of light was intended as a warning and benefit, the Dharma Master redoubled his efforts and responded to it.
When the site was excavated,
a stone casket was indeed found; when the stupa was completed,
it likewise consisted of seven tiers, corresponding to those prior omens.
Yet these people no longer fished.
It was during the Master’s hundred-day practice of repentance at Mount Dongye that a great drought occurred,
such that water was insufficient for use.
He then went out from his quarters to examine it;
suddenly, he struck it with his mendicant’s staff,
whereupon a spring of water gushed forth from the rock.
The so-called Shiyuan Spring (Stone-Eye Spring) in the eastern gate-tower today is that very place.
Initially, the people of Hangzhou wished to invite the Dharma Master to cross to the west to preach the Dharma;
although messengers traveled back and forth for seven years, he never once accompanied them.
Furthermore, Zhaoqing Qi-yi led the assembly to request him once more before he finally came;
by this time, twelve years had already passed.
Prior to this, the Dharma Master had previously dreamed that he was in his mother’s womb for twelve years.
He calculated the date of his departure and entered Hangzhou;
this was indeed the fulfillment of his dream.
Upon arriving in Hangzhou, he stayed at Zhaokong Temple and extensively propagated the teachings through lectures.
Students flocked to him with great enthusiasm, like water flowing toward a marsh.
In the local customs of Hangzhou, it was customary to hold banquets of wine and delicacies at funerals;
the Dharma Master specifically used this excellent opportunity to exhort them [to reform].
The entire populace was transformed;
they generally changed their consumption of pungent foods for vegetarianism.
Consequently, he composed a written work stating:
He established the Dharma-gate of Abstaining from Alcohol and Meat through Compassion and Wisdom to rectify this matter;
his followers have continued to revere it to this day.
The following year, the people of Su welcomed him with the official seal of their prefecture.
The Dharma Master proceeded to the Kaiyuan Monastery, where he devoted himself day and night to lecturing on the Dharma assembly,
gathering a vast congregation of both monastics and laypeople as listeners.
It is said that ten thousand [people] by day and a thousand by night—
those who did not drink wine or eat meat—
nearly filled the city and its suburbs.
The wine official and the butcher found that their wares were selling poorly.
They then said to their followers,
"Our ancestor Zhi left behind a letter to Prince Jin expressing six regrets."
The first is that it may, by gathering the masses through the Dharma-assembly, cause disturbances and create trouble for the government.
My virtue is now meager;
how could I continue to preside over this assembly? I shall depart from it.
He then turned back and returned to Hangzhou.
It was the year Yiwu of the Xiangfu era.
The Prefect, Lord Xue Yan, appointed him to reside at the hermitage on Mount Ling.
In the past, the Dharma Master had delighted in its magnificent scenery and already harbored the intention to retire there;
thus, this was the fulfillment of his long-cherished wish.
That site was originally the Tianzhu Monastery established by the Sui dynasty’s eminent monk Zhen guan.
It passed through the Tang dynasty, where Dao biao succeeded him;
yet, more than four hundred years having elapsed since the Sui and Tang, the traces left by Master Guan had fallen into oblivion.
It was almost impossible to see.
The Dharma Master consulted ancient records and searched within the vast, desolate wilderness; indeed, he discovered its traces.
He immediately composed a poem and erected a stele to commemorate it.
This was the beginning of the plan to restore [the temple] to its former state in India.
Initially, to the west of the temple stood a cypress planted during the Sui dynasty;
only its withered trunk remained.
Having reached this point, it flourished once again;
this was indeed proof of the temple's reconstruction.
Consequently, it was named the "Re-flourishing Cypress."
Furthermore, he used the plum blossoms upon the rocks at the mouth of the Incense Forest Cave.
As for the bamboo on the mountain’s inner slopes and the bamboo facing the stone surfaces,
together with the cypresses, these constitute the Four Auspicious Omens of Tiantai.
He composed four poems to record their extraordinary excellence.
Before long, those who came to study there increased even more,
so he established Rizhuan Hermitage to the east of that temple.
In the ninth year of the Xiangfu era,
he compiled the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of India* (*Zhantan gao seng zhuan*) and supplemented the teachings on the "Method for the Practice of Samādhi" by Zhiyi to correct the practitioners.
The Monastic Rectifier (Sengzheng) Hui of Tiantai learned of his arrival at the capital and reported his name to the throne;
he was subsequently granted the purple robe.
Soon thereafter, he was invited to lecture at Shouchang Temple.
Upon concluding his lectures, he passed by the former East Gate and said to his disciples:
Mount Ling is the place where I have chosen to spend my final years.
Upon my departure, I shall return there;
meanwhile, I take up my brush to inscribe this long song upon the wall.
Taking leave of the Eastern Gate, he returned to India.
During the summer retreat, he exhorted his disciples to collectively perform the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* repentance ritual.
A year was calculated as a cycle of seven days and nights.
Having grown old, Palace Protector Duke Ma increasingly devoted himself to Buddhism and especially admired the words of the Dharma Master.
He subsequently composed the *Jingtu jueyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Pure Land).
Lord Ma had it carved into printing blocks and circulated it.
Later, when Lord Wang Wenmu retired from the相位 (prime ministership) to serve as the Governor of Hangzhou, he [promoted its distribution].
Having heard of his lofty character, he was invited by Li Mingzhou to meet him at the governor’s residence.
Upon meeting him,
Lord Wang marveled at his extraordinary qualities.
Within a few days, he led his subordinates to visit the Dharma Master in the mountains and immediately commanded him to preach;
the Master then expounded the wondrous meaning of the threefold dharma of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
His talent and eloquence were so clear and brilliant that the gentry and officials turned their eyes toward him.
The Prince remarked,
"I have never heard of such a thing before."
He then cited the fundamental and derivative aspects of Tiantai doctrine, wishing to have them extolled.
The Prince agreed and subsequently memorialized the throne to restore the temple.
I have been granted the title of "Indian," and the prince has inscribed it upon my banner;
this is to honor the sovereign's command.

The reason the Prince first proposed that West Lake be established as a sanctuary for the release of living beings was also because he was moved by the Dharma Master’s exhortation based on the spirit of Zhiyi’s protection of life. At that time,
the Prince, who had been appointed as the Governor of Yingtian, was slightly unwell.
They met in a dream, and his illness was immediately cured;
he then sent him a letter, describing the matter in detail and stating that their meeting during his lifetime was a most auspicious karmic connection.
He moved to Jiangning and was further welcomed at the official residence.
He stayed there for nearly three months while inquiring about the Dharma.
It was only then that the Prince first intended to have an image of Saṃgha made.
Doubting yet unable to reach a conclusion,
the Dharma Master then explained to him that the responsive manifestations of Avalokiteśvara are all-pervasive and boundless.
Prior to this, the Dharma Master had once dreamed that he and the Prince were together within a Buddhist stupa.
There was an elderly monk who split a golden bell between the two men.
Fayi cited this to verify his previous argument.
The Prince said:
This was truly what one would expect from Jinling.
Once the image was completed, he presented it to the Dharma Master,
and subsequently composed the ritual text for the Venerable of Sizhou to honor the matter.
King Gongyi and his consort, Lady Qin, donated more than six million coins for the construction of the main hall of that monastery.
The Dharma Master used these funds to restore the temple.
It was from the imperial house and the princes that he felt a particular resonance;
consequently, he returned once more to Tiantai and encouraged his disciples to practice the ritual of worshipping the Buddha according to the four seasons.
Desiring to repay his virtue,
he happened upon the Qianyuan Festival;
the King and Dukes reported his path to the Emperor above.
He was subsequently bestowed with the title "Compassionate Cloud" (Ciyun).
From then on, they engaged in spiritual excursions beyond the mundane world with ever-increasing intimacy;
their mutual affection was expressed extensively through poetry and prose.
As for his authored works, such as the *Diagram and Commentary on the Ten Dharma Realms of the Perfect and Sudden* and the *Verses on the Essential Teachings of Master Huisi of Nanyue*,

Yet Master Han’s view differs in this way,
much like the monkey keeper who assigned chestnuts, saying: "Three in the morning and four in the evening," or "Four in the morning and three in the evening."
How could the result possibly differ?
To say that "man" is the lord of the barbarians and beasts is again a confused and vague claim;
it is insufficient to serve as a moral lesson.
If Master Han simply asserts that humans are the masters of their own vital breath (qi),
then those barbarians are likewise human;
they too should naturally be the masters of birds and beasts.
How can it be said that humans are the masters of birds and beasts?
Yet even birds and beasts do not have humans as their masters;
each of the myriad species has its own master.
Humans take themselves as masters over their own kind;
even birds and beasts likewise take themselves as masters over their own kind.
How could there be any birds or beasts in the world that tame and familiarize themselves with humans to serve as their masters?
If that Master Han were truly concerned for the Yi and Di and for birds and beasts—
regarding them as sharing the same nature and life as himself—
he would desire that people not treat them with violence.
Regarding the origin of this matter, one should say: "Human beings share their life with the barbarians and the beasts.
While they share the same life, those who are violent toward that life have failed to attain the Way by which one ought to live."
If this were so, it would perhaps be acceptable.
Fifth: Master Han’s "On Fundamental Government" states:
"The government of the Zhou was ornate."
Once it had fallen into decay,
later generations did not know its origins,
yet they widely propagated the teachings of the ancient sages.
He then employed the arts of his time to clearly instruct the people;
thus, the people first became confused by the teachings of the hundred schools, which then flourished.
It is further said:
I heard from my teacher that those who ruled the world in antiquity transformed it through their influence,
yet they did not reveal the specific way by which they effected that transformation.
When these reach their exhaustion, they are changed;
yet the Way by which they are changed is not revealed.
Thus the administration gains the people, and through this, the people become pure.
Those who undertake this task shall understand the origins of edification and its decline;
they shall suppress the bizarre and strange while promoting the Imperial Ultimate (Huangji),
and humble literary affectations to honor loyalty and substance.
Vast is the movement of Heaven; profound is the transformation of the Spirit.
Is it not here that the Way may truly be realized?
Is this statement by Master Han not perhaps an excessive aversion to the faults of literary embellishment?
He was one who left traces of his teachings.
Yet his words seem to desire that the world follow the governance of the Three Kings so that the ornate and the substantial may mutually remedy one another;
furthermore, they appear to desire that the world follow the Three Sovereigns so that the Way of ease and simplicity may serve as the means of transformation.
His words lack any clear basis and cause students to be perplexed.
If Master Han truly desires to emulate the governance of the Three Kings, [he must clarify his principles].
How could the Three Kings not have demonstrated the way by which they governed?
If one truly desires to be as non-action as the Three Kings,
it must be like the vast turning of Heaven and the profound, mysterious transformation of the spirit.
This is similar to what Laozi refers to as his "Dao and De.
It is like the ancient rulers who governed the world through transformation,
yet did not reveal the specific means by which they effected that transformation.
Nothing is more magnificent than the Three Sovereigns—Fuxi, Shennong, and Huangdi.
These Three Sovereigns are precisely those whom the Master Lao takes as his teachers and paragons for his Way.
When Master Han criticizes Laozi, claiming that his discourse on the Dao and its Virtue is merely the private speech of a single individual, he is mistaken.
If the teachings of Laozi were indeed private,
how could these words of Master Han be considered public? How is it that Master Han,
in composing his book, was so lacking in reflection and so careless in his judgment?
How can scholars examine this and take it as a standard?

Sixth: The sixth chapter, "Explaining Ghosts" (Yuangui), composed by Hanzi, was written because he encountered a time when the people were beset by such occurrences; thus, he explained ghosts in order to debate the matter.
Alas! Why must one seek the origins of ghosts?
If the people do not know of ghosts, what harm is there to the administration of government?
But if the people come to know of ghosts...
What benefit would there be even in teaching?
The gentlemen of antiquity used the Way to discern delusion and governance to pacify calamities;
it was simply this.
In ancient times, the administration of Yin was corrupt and its people worshipped ghosts.

The former kings were concerned by this and sought to suppress it; "suppressing" (sha) here may actually mean "saving" (jiao). Those referred to as "ghost-worshippers" (yi gui zhe) were so called because they possessed many ritual observances that resembled the service of spirits and deities.
Moreover, as for the "Investigation of Ghosts" (Yuan gui),
it truly uses ghosts to deceive the people;
how could this be the law of the former kings?
The saying goes:
"If one cannot yet serve the living, how can one serve the spirits?
The words of Master Han do not merely contradict the Way of the former kings; they subvert it entirely.
Furthermore, this is a failure to understand the meaning of Confucius;
how utterly erroneous it is!
Seventh: The seventh [section], Hanzi’s “Explanation of the Capture of the Qilin,” says:
When the qilin appears, there must be a sage occupying the throne;
the qilin appears for the sake of the sage.
A sage must, of necessity, know the qilin.
The appearance of the qilin is not an ill omen;
this refers to the qilin appearing for the sake of Confucius.
Confucius knew the qilin.
The qilin is an auspicious omen;
this is intended to resolve the ancient view of the people of Lu who claimed that the qilin was an inauspicious portent.
As for what Master Han [Fei] says, it shows he has not yet understood the Classics.

The reason the *麒麟* (qilin) appears in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (*Chunqiu*) is that if one cannot elucidate the intent behind Confucius’s composition of the *Chunqiu*, what use is there in explaining the appearance of the qilin?
As for the qilin, even a student of learning would be able to discern its significance.
Confucius was a sage;
how could he have known only the *qilin*?
To say that the appearance of the *qilin* signified the emergence of Confucius—this is [a mere interpretation].
To simply take up the reckless assertions of miscellaneous schools (zajia) is a fallacious argument lacking scriptural authority.
When Master Han [Dai] spoke of knowing the Sage and praising the qilin,
he did not do so merely because of its appearance or non-appearance.
In ancient times, when Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (*Chunqiu*) upon encountering the qilin,
it was because the four auspicious creatures— the qilin and the phoenix— are generally dependent upon the royal administration.
Thus, the *Liyun* says:
When the sages established their models, they took the four spiritual beings as their domestic animals.
At the time of Confucius,
the House of Zhou had long been in decline and the Way of the King was already severed.
There was the qilin, yet there was no righteous governance.
Moved by this, the Sage [Confucius] thereby determined his course, intending to preserve the royal laws.
Thus his writings began with King Ping and concluded with the capture of the qilin.
However, Du Yu’s commentary on the "Acquisition of the Qilin" is vague and inconclusive; it states:
The qilin is an auspicious omen of a sage-king.
It is also said:
"In these times, there is no enlightened king."
One perceives auspicious omens yet there is no response;
since there is no enlightened king,
by what means could such an appearance be brought about?
This is likely because Du [Yi] was unable to examine the meaning of whether [the text] originated from him or not.
In the "Liyun" (The Course of Ritual), Confucius stated:
"The governance of the sage-kings was one of great accordance with the Way."
Therefore, phoenixes and qilins were all found in the wilds and marshes;
tortoises and dragons were in the palace ponds.
"Wilds" refers to those areas bordering the royal city.
"Thicket" refers to the shallow clusters used for firewood.
To say that what is moved by Great Accordance is like the qilin and phoenix being kept as domesticated animals means that they appear in accordance with such cultivation.
These words concern nothing more than firewood gathered in the vicinity of the capital.
Such is what they say regarding the appearance of the *qilin*.
The *Zuozhuan* states:
While hunting in the great marsh of Daye in the west, he captured a qilin.
Daye was likely the vast marsh of Lu;
it was wild, remote, and steeply isolated.
Consider the Yunmeng marshes of Chu and the Jiqu lake of Wu;
these are all that the world calls the ten great marshes.
Yet deep mountains and vast lakes are naturally the places where extraordinary creatures lie hidden.
The qilin was unfortunately captured by the men of Lu and brought forth; how could it have appeared of its own accord out of some spiritual resonance?
Therefore I say:
the qilin has never actually appeared; to claim that this [creature] was the appearance of a qilin is a misconception.
If that were so, then the words of Confucius in the "Run of Rites" (Liyun) would be erroneous.
How could a sage be mistaken?
The Classic says:
"The Qilin was captured during a hunt in the west;
it can be known that the Qilin appeared not of its own accord.
The Sage recorded this with his brush."
This does not mean that it is not good.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, whenever the term "captured" (huò) is used,
it is not solely defined as "to obtain."
This refers to the meaning of being powerful in arms and victorious in battle.
It is exemplified by the passage in the Classic [the *Spring and Autumn Annals*] concerning the capture of the Marquis of Jin.
The present mention of "hunting in the west" is intended to express disapproval of hunting at an improper time and the resulting violence toward living creatures;
the capture of the qilin is merely an occasion for this censure.
Those who hold differing views say:
"Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
establishing his words as the law for a 'plain king' (a king without the mandate of Heaven)."
The qilin then appeared in response.
Some say that its appearance is an auspicious omen for prosperity, while its absence is a calamity signaling decline.
To claim that the qilin serves as an auspicious omen for those who receive the Mandate in future generations is something not recorded in the classics or commentaries.
To judge such matters based on mere personal conjecture is utterly unworthy of acceptance.
To claim that Confucius was a "plain king" (sowang) is an extreme instance of calumniating the Sage.
Eighth: Hanzi presented himself for recommendation by means of three writings.
Seeking employment as a high minister,
I have never failed to sigh with admiration whenever I read his works.
The world says that Master Han was a sage-like worthy who emerged as a successor to the Holy One.
I maintain that the advancement and withdrawal, speech and silence, and movements of the sages and worthies always possess a teacher’s method;
they should not sink or float along with ordinary men.
The scholars of antiquity all desired to be employed.
He would not employ anyone whose conduct did not accord with the rites.
Among the scholars of the Three Dynasties who took the governance of the world upon themselves as their responsibility,
none was like Yi Yin.
At the end of the Zhou dynasty, no one was more concerned for the world than Confucius;
during the era of the Warring States, he sought to put his Way into practice.
There was none like Mencius.
Nevertheless, although both were appointed to office through the ritual of invitation (*li*),
we have never heard of them seeking employment by presenting their own writings for self-recommendation.
The *Li* says: "The Ru possesses treasures upon his mat to await an invitation;
he studies diligently day and night to await inquiry;
and he harbors loyalty and good faith to await being raised up."
Exert yourself in practice to await their attainment.
As the saying goes:
"The Master attained it through being mild, kind, respectful, frugal, and deferential."
"In the Master's seeking of it,
was it perhaps different from the way others seek it?
Chenzi said to Mencius:
"How did the gentlemen of antiquity serve in office?
Mencius replied,
"There were three reasons for which they accepted service, and three reasons for which they departed."
If one receives them with respectful greetings and proper ritual decorum, and their words are about to be put into practice, then one approaches them.
If the ritual courtesy has not yet declined but their words are not being practiced, then one departs from them, and so forth.
Now, the sages and worthies of antiquity waited for things rather than seeking them.
To wait thus without seeking was because they prized righteousness and maintained the Way.
This is precisely what makes them sages and worthies.
Since Master Han was unable to preserve the Way and honor righteousness as the sages and worthies of antiquity did,
he furthermore sought to recommend himself to his superior by means of this letter.
It is surely appropriate to respect their words and maintain a tranquil demeanor; one may simply follow one's own path.
How could one be so impetuous and angry as to hastily condemn the governance of others?
Confucius said:
To speak before one has reached the point of doing so is called "restlessness.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The arrogance of today is characterized by resentment and perversity. Hanzi extrapolated from the deeds of the Duke of Zhou to compare the governance of his era with that of his own time.
It is not that they have failed to arrive.
Now, to immediately mock the administration before one has even reached a position of office—
is this not impetuous?
To fail to examine oneself while holding others accountable—
is this not an indulgence in anger?
The *Ruxing* says:
He cleansed his person and bathed in virtue;
he set forth his words and prostrated himself,
remaining still and rectifying his mind.
The superior man does not know this;
he treats it as coarse and merely raises it up,
nor does he act with urgency.
"Presenting one's words and then prostrating" means that when a Confucian has something to expound,
he must invariably prostrate himself while awaiting the command of his superior.
"To remain tranquil and maintain correctness" means that even if one does not receive the mandate [of office], one must remain tranquil and uphold it,
maintaining correctness without succumbing to instability or agitation.

"Superiors do not know what is coarse, yet they hold it aloft and do not act upon it with urgency" means that even though one possesses virtuous words and correct conduct, if superiors do not recognize them,
one merely matches their facial expression and issues them in a perfunctory manner.
One need not act with haste or violence;
this is what the Sage meant by such words.
It was intended that people would follow the Way and distance themselves from disgrace.
Adherence to ritual is what defines a Confucian.
Master Han admired Confucius and claimed to be a pure Confucian,
yet his own actions were contrary to the laws of the Sage in this very manner.
Can he truly be called a Confucian?
Not only has he failed to reach the standard of a Confucian,
but I fear he will also mislead future generations.
When a person loses propriety, they invite disgrace.
In the book of Master Han, he desires that the court utilize his own rank and emolument to attract and entice the reclusive scholars of the world.
How shallow and erroneous it is for Master Han to judge the world by such words! Indeed,
there are those in the world who do not fall into despondency through poverty and low station, nor succumb to arrogance through wealth and honor.
Those who were truly able to preserve the Way and,
maintaining their integrity, excelled in virtue even beyond Hanzi—
such as Fu Yue, Zhuge Liang, and their like.
How could Fu Yue and Zhuge Liang have suddenly come merely because of others,
or have they wandered about seeking profit and reward?
This has been but a brief mention of those most renowned and well-known in their respective eras.
At such a time, a ruler may attract those who possess the capacity for great achievement by employing ritual propriety, righteousness, and sincerity;
how much more so those who have submerged their names and severed their traces,
having escaped the net of the world?
Indeed, there have been those like Bo Bo and Boyi who regarded the division of a kingdom as no more than a grain of sand or a tiny weight,
refusing to serve as ministers or hold office;
even if they were offered rank and titles a hundred times over, they would have treated them with utter disdain.
How could Master Han possibly entice and bring them here?
I fear that Master Han’s strategy may not necessarily enable the state to obtain those who are most virtuous.
Hanzi says:
"In ancient times, if a man did not hold office for three months, they would mourn for one another.
This quotation refers to the beginning of the chapter on the lower section of the *Teng Wen Gong* in Mencius, which records the initial response to Zhou Xiao's question.
The Master Han merely abridges the words of Mencius—some editions read "abridges" as "plunders"—and is thus unable to fully convey his meaning.
At the conclusion of that chapter, Mencius says:
"In ancient times, men never failed to desire office."
Furthermore, evil does not proceed by the proper Way; those who proceed without following the Way are of the same category as those who bore holes through walls and peep through cracks.
This statement precisely means that although a scholar may be urgent in seeking office, [he must still act according to principle].
One must also wait for their mandate before employing them;
one must not seek employment through reckless advancement.
Those who seek employment through reckless advancement—
It is certainly true that when men and women do not await the commands of their parents or the words of matchmakers,
but instead peer through holes and crevices or climb over walls to follow one another,
they become objects of contempt for others.
Now, Master Han has recommended himself and sought employment;
yet he cites this chapter of Mencius as an analogy.
How can he so suddenly manifest his own lack of propriety and loss of righteousness?
I have heard that in antiquity, when one wished to have an audience,
one did so solely by presenting the appropriate gift (*zhi*).
For the Son of Heaven, the gift was fragrant wine (*chang*).
The feudal lords presented jade as their gift;
the high ministers presented lambs;
and the great officers presented wild geese.
A scholar presents a pheasant as his introductory gift.
Thus Mencius said:
"When Confucius went beyond the borders of his state, he invariably carried a sacrificial offering."
It was not that they did not hear of those who had seen [the texts] above through books;
rather, it was because people of later generations acted with such negligence.
This was during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty.
Scholars from the four quarters, such as Dongfang Shuo and his like,
were arrogant and boastful,
seeking to sell themselves by presenting their writings as recommendations for employment.
The world then emulates one another until it becomes a prevailing custom.
Mencius spoke of "selling oneself to serve as a ruler," yet those who cherish their integrity within their local communities would not do such a thing.
Yet you claim that the worthy ones did this.
But who among them has ever felt ashamed because of it? Alas!
In later generations, the world grew increasingly decadent, and the moral teachings became ever more frivolous and superficial.
Among scholars, they boast of their arts and vie with one another for their skills;
who among them is not arrogant and self-important?
The Way of benevolence, gentleness, respectfulness, frugality, and deference was nearly abandoned.
At such a time, Master Han ought indeed to have diligently practiced the Way of the Sage,
leading the world by personal example and rectifying its customs.
Furthermore, as they engage in these practices, their self-importance, arrogance, anger, and impetuosity grow ever more intense.
Those of later generations study them without knowing the fundamental principles;
seeing only the writings of Hanzi, they say to one another:
Hanzi was a great Confucian scholar;
we ought to emulate his conduct.
By doing so, not only will it benefit our moral instruction, but it will also diminish [the influence of] heterodox teachings.
Furthermore, it harms the integrity of one's ministers and brings disgrace upon the person themselves;
hence it is said:
"The writings of Master Han (Han Fei) do not accord with the Dharma;
I have nothing to take from them.
Someone said:
In the time of Master Han,
the way he recruited officials differed from that of antiquity;
Master Han likely acted in accordance with the exigencies of his own era.
If one must strictly adhere to the Way of antiquity,
waiting for an invitation before entering service,
then the Way of the scholar-gentleman will surely remain unpracticed until death.
I say: it is not so.
Master Han still uses the way of the Duke of Zhou to hold the ministers of his own time accountable;
how could he possibly fail to consider this?
The present age differs from antiquity;
one cannot seek the present by means of ancient ways.
Is it not the case that while planning for oneself is called "acting according to the times," holding others accountable is called "requiring them to conform strictly to ancient ways"?
If the gentleman truly intends this,
then what age has not possessed the ritual of recruiting scholars?
Even in the Tang dynasty, we still hear of those who were summoned from their seclusion by means of the ritual.
How could there be any sage or worthy whom he has failed to invite?
As the saying goes:
"One does not worry about lacking a position; one worries about how one establishes oneself."
"Do not worry that others do not know you; strive instead to be worthy of being known.
This is a point that the followers of Master Han (Han Fei) should also reflect upon.

Yu transmitted the empire to Yi;
Yi yielded it to Qi,

He debated and adjudicated these matters in order to rectify those throughout the world who engaged in groundless slander;
yet, his aspirations remained unfulfilled.
However, as for me now, being already fifty years of age,
I am close to death;
thus, in the end, I shall not be able to do so.
Perhaps among my followers there may be one sage.
Given that the present Emperor is enlightened and sagacious and the court is supremely impartial,
in days to come he will surely take up my book and present it for deliberation.
Thus, you have not brought shame upon those who serve my Way.
